source_data.original_text:
Situated at the edge of an area of flat enclosed pasture, to immediate E, S and SE (c. 32m) of a shingle beach on the E shores of Killala Bay (7m OD). The surrounding area consists of enclosed pasture of linear fields defined by wire fences that are built over collapsed earlier rubble stone field boundary walls. The signal tower site has unobstructed views in all directions. Creevagh Signal Tower (MA007-015002-), located c. 14.8kms to the W\WSW, has been demolished and can no longer be seen from the site. The upper levels of Rathlee Signal Tower (SL011-025001-), located c. 1.7kms to the SSE, are visible from this site. The view to the well-preserved Carrowmably\Carrowmabla Signal Tower (SL012-08003-), located c. 12kms to the ESE, is now obscured by intervening trees. Signal tower located c. 576m NNW of the remains of a probable late medieval church (SL010-024----) and burial ground (SL010-024001-) at Carrowmacbryan. 

The remains of an early nineteenth-century (c. 1804-6) two-storey square-plan signal tower. The signal station consists of the low fragmentary remains of the signal tower, built with roughly coursed limestone rubble (int. dims. 4.32 SW-NE x 4.57 NW-SE; wall H. 3.48m). The structure is in poor condition with none of the fragmentary walls surviving above ground floor level. The SE wall has the typical shallow outwards bulge to chimney flue. A chute passes through the SW part of the SE wall, sloping down steeply as it passes through the body of the wall. These features allow for the likely orientation of the signal tower to be determined; the SE wall would have housed the central fireplaces (with chimneystack above parapet level) with the flanking alcoves to the ground and first floor levels, the NW wall would have featured the first floor doorway, and the NE and SW walls would have featured pairs of window openings at ground floor and first floor levels. Internally, the SW wall features a poorly-preserved slot with some joist holes that would have held the timber floor structure at ground floor level.  It is possible that the construction of this signal tower was halted during construction, and that the site was changed to nearby Rathlee (SL011-025001-), located to the SE, where a signal tower was then completed (Moore & Robinson 2014, 19).    

The remains of a probable lime kiln are located 14.5m W of the signal tower, which was possibly used during the construction of this site. The probable kiln (ext. dims 2.9m E-W x 1.7m N-S) consists of a shallow oval depression filled with loose random rubble stones. A few small sections of intact stonework can be seen around the sides of the kiln. Collapsed rubble stone field walls (Wth c. 1.6m; H. c. 0.3m) connect to the signal tower at its N and S corners. These survive only as grassed-over banks of collapsed rubble stone. 

The signal tower was part of a system of over 80 signal stations constructed by the British Board of Ordnance in the first decade of the 19th century to warn of the approach of a French invasion fleet. Signalling between sites was accomplished using a naval signal post. The system formed a continuous chain from Dublin Bay running clockwise all the way around the coast to Malin Head in County Donegal. It was abandoned by the mid-1810s when the threat of a French invasion diminished (Kerrigan 1995, 157-66).

Compiled by: Stuart Rathbone

source_data.original_text:
Situated on the S bank of the mouth of the Leaffony River on the E shore of Killala Bay. Marked on the Down Survey (1655-6) map and on all OS editions of the OS 6-inch map. The OS recorded that the castle is believed to have been erected by the O'Dowds and was called 'Caislean poll a-chaonnaigh' or 'The castle of the hole of the moss' (OS Name Book (1837), 453). Part of the castle was still standing at that time. It was 'about three stories high' and appeared to have been 'built solely for strength'. A number of legends and placenames associated with the castle were also recorded. The site has been destroyed. Present remains comprise a circular, low, flat-topped mound (diam. 14m; H 1.4m). Much of the W and the N sides have been destroyed and are overlain by a modern roadway. The S side is truncated by a deep drain. Two deep quarry holes have been dug into the mound. There is no masonry now visible. (OS Letters 1836, 294 (119); O'Rorke 1890, 418; ITA Survey 1942-4).

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight rise overlooking the E shore of Killala Bay. The OS Letters (1836, 292 (119)) and O'Rorke (1890, 418-9) recorded that this castle was constructed in 1560 by the MacFirbis'. Wood-Martin (1882, 106) concurs with the latter date but asserts that it was constructed by the O'Dowds 'and in consequence of the events of 1641 was fortified by them, and granted to the family of Wood'. Present remains comprise a mound (10.5m E-W; c. 6m N-S; max. H 1.4m) of rubble and stone blocks, bisected by a modern E-W field boundary wall. The basal portion of the walls at S (H 0.6m) and at E (L 6m; H 1.1m; T 0.8m) are still visible. A low bank (7m E-W; Wth 2.8m; H 0.4m) may mark the line of the N wall. A break in centre of the S wall (Wth. 0.88m) may mark the location of the original entrance.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Located in flat, lowlying poorly drained coastal pasture, traversed by a network of field drains.  When first recorded in 1993 this fulacht fia appeared as a low irregular-shaped mound (c. 10m N-S; c. 9m E–W) of heat-shattered stone and charcoal, which had been suffered disturbance in the past. The N end of the mound was markedly higher and incorporated a small semicircular depression (Wth 0.6m N–S). A raised rim or scarp (H 0.5m) defined the S edge of the mound. The limits of the mound along its W and E edges were more irregular and difficult to trace. An inspection in 2013 found that the mound is extant but has been graded-off somewhat during land improvement works, and now appears as a low, roughly circular rise (12m N–S; 11m E–W; H 0.5-0.6m). The N end of the mound is highest (H 0.5-0.6m) and a low scarp can be traced N–SE but elsewhere the limits of the mound are less clearly defined and grade seamlessly into the surrounding field surface.

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture of long grass and yellow flag, in lowlying coastal terrain. Not listed in the SMR (1989) but listed as ‘moated site -possible’ in the RMP (1995) on the basis of a subrectangular feature noted in an aerial photograph (GSI G 103-4; Roll 157, print 14). The area was inspected in 2014. The feature noted in the aerial photograph corresponds to a roughly oval or subrectangular area (c. 25m NW–SE; c. 10-14m NE–SW) of flat ground, marked by shorter grass than elsewhere in the field, with a limekiln (SL010-031002-) at the NE end of the area. The S side of the flat area is defined by a slight scarp (H 0.3m) which curves in a shallow arc from the lime kiln for c. 25m to SW where it peters out in dense vegetation. The N side of the flat area is marked by a linear band (Wth c. 1m) of yellow flag. Another linear band of yellow flag extends from the limekiln for c. 10m to SW roughly through the centre of the flat area. The evidence does not warrant classifying this as a moated site. It is possible that the remains represent a levelled enclosure, or they may simply be the result of past cultivation/drainage activity associated with the limekiln. There is a moated site (SL010-019----) 75m to W.

source_data.original_text:
This souterrain was discovered in 2002 when workmen displaced a roof stone while undertaking ground clearance works in advance of the construction of a house. The exposed hole revealed a souterrain chamber of drystone construction, roofed by stone lintels. The polygonal-shaped chamber (2.4m NW–SE; 2.2m NE–SW; H c. 2m) has a narrow lintelled opening at its SE end which leads to a short passage (L 1.5m NW–SE) on the same alignment as the chamber. A narrow opening at the S corner of this passage leads into a second passage (L 6m NE-SW; Wth c. 1m), which extends at right angles to SW. Roughly mid-way along the SE wall of this passage there is a blocked up creepway (Wth 0.45m; H 0.4m). At its SW end, the second passage opens into a third passage (Wth c. 0.9m) which extends at right angles to it for c. 3.2m to SE. The souterrain underlies the house and a modern road which fronts the E side of the house.

source_data.original_text:
Named Castletown Castle on the OS 6-inch maps. Post-medieval fortification, probably of 17th century date. Situated on a rock outcrop on the W side of the estuary of the River Easky. Subrectangular, single-storey, split-level structure (L of N wall 9.9m; L of E wall 22.4m; L of S wall 8.7m; L of W wall 20.9m; Wall T 0.78-1.25m). The smaller, lower level is rectangular in plan (int. dims. 7.6m N-S; 3.3m E-W) and projects out 1.7m over the estuary. It contains a gun port and nine musket loops. A cross-wall divides this room from the larger upper level wihich is subrectangular in plan (int. dims. c. 11.8m N-S; c. 4m E-W) and featureless. Immediately N of these rooms is a third, rectangular room (int. dims. c. 5.7m E-W; c. 3m N-S) which is largely filled with collapse. Between 0.4m and 5.9m out from the W and N sides of this latter room is a low, curving bank of earth and stone (Wth. 1.45-4m; H 0.25-0.4m) which probably marks the circuit of a bawn wall (SL011-019001-).

source_data.original_text:
Overlooking the sea to the N and the estuary of the River Easky to the W. The OS Letters (1836, 283 (115)), 286-7 (116-7)) recorded that the castle was built by Oliver McDonnell in 1207 and it remained in the possession of that family until 1549. In 1603, the first year of the reign of King James 1, it was granted to Daniel O'Dowd. A contemporary description of the property recorded '2 castles, a kitchen and bakehouse within the bawn of Roslee' (ITA Survey 1942-4, 11). A late 18th-century plan and drawing depicts a rectangular keep with an adjoining building, aligned E-W, at the E side. The adjoining building is rectangular in plan, longer and narrower than the keep. Extending N from the NW angle of the keep is a length of bawn wall (Grose 1797, vol. 1, 59). Only the keep now survives. This comprises a three-storey rectangular structure (12.05m E-W; 9m N-S - Wall T 2.05m) with a slight base batter. The original entrance (Wth. 1.65m), now blocked up, is at the N end of the E wall. The present entrance, formerly a window embrasure, is in the centre of the S wall. The E 1/3 of the barrel vault which covers ground-floor level is absent. A mural stairway, commencing at the N end of the E wall and returning S, gives access to the first-floor level. In the centre of the E wall, at first-floor level, is a large blocked-up window. There are also single-light windows in the S, W and N walls. There is a garderobe in the NW angle. A mural stairs in the S wall rises directly to the battlement level. Access to the second-floor level must, therefore, have been by a wooden stairway. The second-floor level is lit by windows in S and W walls only. Casey (1999, 195, P3) noted this as a potential promontory fort but on inspection, apart from some bumps and hollows inland of the tower house, there was no evidence to suggest that it was the site of an earlier promontory fort.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

source_data.original_text:
In Easkey village, located on bedrock bluff c. 20m N of Easkey River. Enclosed on the S and W by an L-shaped, walled graveyard (SL011-021001-). Indicated on the 1837 OS 6-inch map as 'Abbey' and on the 1913 edition as 'Abbey in Ruins'. The church is listed in the Ecclesiastical Taxation of Ireland of 1306 as Imelackiskel and is valued at 5 marks (Sweetman and Handcock (eds) 1886, 217; O’Rorke 1889, 414). 
Ruined rectangular church, with walls of mortared random rubble. The E and W gables and the S wall survive to almost full height. The E end of the N wall has fallen and the surviving lower courses were capped with concrete blocks. There is a narrow window, now partly broken out, in the W gable. The E gable features a tall, round-headed lancet window (H 2.4m; Wth 0.21m) in an inwardly splayed embrasure (Wth 1.6m). The embrasure is capped with a lintel made from whale bone (Moore 2016, 3). Another round-headed lancet at the E end of the S wall is blocked up in the interior wall face, but remains clearly visible on the exterior. The doorway (H 1.85m; Wth 1.65m) is located to W of centre in the S wall. In a drawing of the church done by Wakeman in 1879, the doorway is surmounted by a hood moulding incorporating three carved stone heads, with the head at the apex of the arch depicting a mitred bishop (Wakeman 1893, folio 121, no. 153). Only two fragments of dressed stone remain in situ on the doorway but, during a graveyard survey in 2015-2016, several displaced fragments of the hood moulding and the lower door frame were found within the graveyard (Moore 2016, 5). Amongst the finds is one of the carved stone heads, now badly damaged. The bishop’s head, with a finely carved decorative band on the mitre, was found several years previously. 
The two lancet windows may date to the 13th century; the hood moulding of the doorway is 15th- or 16-century in date (Moore 2016, 5). A ringed cross is depicted at the apex of the W gable in Wakeman’s 1879 drawing, and was also noted by Wood-Martin (1882, 115) who recorded 'a remarkable cross on the gable of the old church at Easkey'. Two fragments of a carved stone cross were found in 2015 at the base of the interior of the west gable, and may be from this gable cross. They indicate a maximum width of the cross-arms of 0.62m. A rope chord decoration is evident on the outer edge of the cross circle. This cross appears to be relatively late in date (Moore 2016, 14).
The interior floor space of the church is grass-covered, and largely filled with grave slabs, three table tombs, and low, uninscribed grave markers. The design of some of the grave slabs suggests that they date to the 18th century, although the inscriptions are now illegible. An inscription on one of the table tombs dates to the early 19th century. A 19th-century grave in the SE angle encroaches on the S edge of the window in the E gable, and the wall surfaces at E and S in the angle have been covered in cement plaster to a height of c. 1.75m.
A programme of conservation works under the aegis of the Community Monument Fund and Sligo County Council was undertaken at the church in 2021 and 2022.

source_data.original_text:
In Easkey village, located on a low bluff overlooking the Easkey River, which lies c. 25m to E.  Roughly L-shaped walled graveyard (c. 30m NNW-SSE; c. 20m ENE-WSW) which encloses the W and S sides of a late medieval church (SL011-021----). The entrance gate is in the high, stone-built W wall of the graveyard, opening directly off the main street of the village. A low rectangular stone-built bench abutting the outer face of the graveyard wall at NW may have served as a coffin rest (Moore 2016, 5). Within the graveyard are grave slabs, headstones, table tombs and chest tombs, with the greatest density in the N half of the graveyard. Where inscription can be read, the graves date to the 19th century. Interspersed between the formal graves, are rows of low, uninscribed stone grave markers. A stone, which barely protrudes above the ground surface, adjacent to a 19th-century grave in the N half of the graveyard, appears to be a quernstone or millstone, which was reused as a gravemarker (Pers. comm. Tamlyn McHugh, 2019).
In the SW corner of the graveyard is a small rectangular building (int. dims. 4.1m E–W; 3m N–S) with mortared stone walls (H 0.8-1.05m; Wth 0.4-0.6m), probably dating to early 19th century. It is roofless and the walls are partly concealed by ivy. The W gable is incorporated into the W wall of the graveyard. There is a flat-headed doorway in the E gable and a narrow, broken out window towards the W end of the N wall. There is a small stone font set into the inner face of the E wall to N of the doorway. Abutting the W gable are two pedestals (H 0.5m), set 0.72m apart, which appear to have supported an altar. The interior floor space, now grass-grown, is occupied by two grave slabs.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on level ground within the modern dispersed rural settlement of Rathlee (29mOD), and approximately c. 820m ESE of the coastline at its nearest point. Located within enclosed pasture with a minor road to the S. The site has unobstructed views in all directions. Creevagh Signal Tower, Mayo (MA007-015002-), located c. 15.7kms to the WNW, has been demolished and can no longer be seen from the site. The view to the ruinous Lenadoon Point Signal Tower (SL010-001002-), located c. 1.7kms to the NNW, is blocked by intervening buildings; and the view to the well-preserved Carrowmably\Carrowmabla Signal Tower (SL012-008003-), located c. 10.6kms to the ENE, is blocked by intervening forestry. An undated kitchen midden (SL011-025002-) is located 13.5m NE of the signal tower at Rathlee, and the site of a possible souterrain (SL011-096----) is located c. 38m to the NW. 

An early nineteenth-century (c. 1804-6) two-storey square-plan signal tower, built with roughly coursed rubble stone masonry (int. dims. 4.28m N-S x 4.28m E-W; H. c. 11.9m). Extensive sections of roughcast lime render survive to the exterior elevations, particularly to the N, W and E elevations. The N wall features the first floor doorway that would have been accessed via a retractable ladder. This doorway retains a fine cut stone block-and-start surround, cut stone lintel over with central projecting keystone, and a cut stone threshold\sill. A narrow but well-preserved rectangular machicolation is present above the doorway, supported by five small rendered corbels. A row of four small square holes runs across the wall below the doorway at ground floor level, which may be putlog holes used to support scaffolding during the construction of the tower. The two holes in the middle of the N wall are set slightly lower than the outer two holes. Only the inner pair of holes pass through the body of the wall. The E and W walls feature pairs of square-headed windows (with splayed reveals) to the ground floor and first floor levels. The windows to the W elevation at first floor level retain cut stone block-and-start surrounds, cut stone lintels over with central projecting keystones, and cut stone sills, which are now missing to the other window openings. The N ground floor window on the W wall has been opened up to act as a ground level entrance to the structure. The opening has spread northwards and the NE corner of the building is missing from ground level up to the top of the window opening. The S wall bows slightly outwards to house the chimney flue. An intact chimneystack extends from the top of the S wall\parapet, which retains cut stone coping over. There are numerous shallow holes in the S wall, distributed without an obvious pattern. They resemble putlog holes, but may have had a different purpose. Two of the holes pass through the wall and mirror the position of the two central holes on the N wall. Rounded rendered rubble stone bartizans are located on the SE and SW corners of the signal tower, supported by rounded rubble stonework corbels. In the centre of the S wall there is a modern grey incised stone plaque that reads ‘Rathlee Signalling Tower. In memory of those who worked here and all who perished at sea. 2nd July 2006.’ To the right of this is an older white stone [marble] sign that reads ‘Ruin of O’Dowd castle Lochtar Rath a seat of Kings of Tirerach.’ To the right of the white sign there is a large dressed stone block incorporated into the body of the wall. The stone block features a small square hole in its centre. Behind the hole there is a heavy metal sphere that appears to be a small cannon ball, secured in place by a solidly-anchored horizontal metal bar. The painted words ‘Castle Cannon Ball’ are faintly visible on the stone block. It is not thought that any of the signal towers were ever equipped with cannon, so the origin of this object is unclear. 

The internal space consists of a semi-basement level, a ground-floor room with a split mezzanine level, a first-floor room, and a low attic level. The flat roof had been accessible from the first floor level, and a rubble stone parapet wall protects the edge of the roof and connects to the bartizans and the machicolation. No evidence of surviving coping to the parapet wall. The floors and the roof of the building had been wooden and were carried in the thickness of the wall. No parts of the floors or the roof have survived, but rows of joist-holes indicate their former positions. The interior walls feature large sections of surviving lime render. The semi-basement is largely infilled with soil, and is only exposed at the NW corner of the signal tower. The S wall features central square-headed fireplaces at ground and first floors, each with flanking square-headed alcoves.  The ground floor alcoves retain thick layers of render. In the W alcove the impression of four thick shelves are visible in the render. In the E alcove the impression of two shelves are visible at the top of the alcove. A rubble stone seat\plinth with a curved back protruding into the body of the wall occupies the lower part of the east alcove. The two square holes that pass through the central part of the S wall emerge to either side of the top of the fireplace. These holes line up with the two holes that pass through the N wall. The arrangement suggests that two large wooden beams passed through the ground floor room, possibly introduced as a stabilisation measure. 

A well-preserved World War II-era lookout lost (L.O.P. 65) is located 4.9m N of the signal tower. A concrete trigonometry pillar is located 3.3m E of the signal tower. A small lime kiln, which was possibly used during the construction of the tower, is located in a bank 15m to the N of the signal tower. Modern stone walls, paved courtyard opening to roadway to S, and timber seating to S.

The signal tower was part of a system of over 80 signal stations constructed by the British Board of Ordnance in the first decade of the 19th century to warn of the approach of a French invasion fleet. Signalling between sites was accomplished using a naval signal post. The system formed a continuous chain from Dublin Bay running clockwise all the way around the coast to Malin Head in County Donegal. It was abandoned by the mid-1810s when the threat of a French invasion diminished (Kerrigan 1995, 157-66).

In undulating coastal pasture, located on top of a ridge on the W side of a steep-sided, wooded ravine, in the base of which the Ballymeeny river flows N to the sea. Not shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map; shown on the 1913 edition as a semi-circular hachured area, curving SW–SE, and defined on S by a field boundary. This roughly circular enclosure (diam. c. 24m) has been levelled. A slight rise, representing a levelled enclosing bank, can be traced curving SW–NW, changing at N–S to a barely discernible undulation or cropmark. source_data.original_text:
On a rocky ledge on the W slope of a steep-sided, wooded ravine. Thre is a steep fall of ground to the river in the base of the ravine. The well, named 'St. Ernan's Well' on the OS 6-inch maps, and traditionally associated with St. Farannan, consists of a small triangular opening (H 0.3m; Wth 0.4m) in the bedrock through which a spring flows. A rough path leads from the river up the steep slope and then follows the contours of a natural ledge to the well. The path passes a natural rocky shelf, c. 12m to S of the well, which according to tradition, is known as the ‘Saint’s Bed’, where the hermit saint is said to have slept (O’Rorke 1889, vol. 2, 413). According to local information, the traditional ‘pattern’ or pilgrimage to the well was held on Garland Sunday, the last Sunday in July. A natural rock outcrop adjacent to the river, at the base of the E wall of the ravine, was used as an altar (SL011-058001-). Pilgrims crossed the river and climbed the west slope of the ravine to visit the holy well. When returning across the river, they picked up a stone from a natural river pool, known as ‘Dabhach Fharannain’, which was also used as a holy well (SL011-058002-). They then climbed to the the ridge top on the E side of the ravine and deposited the stone on a cairn (SL011-058----), known as the ‘Saint’s Grave’.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 2 July 2013

source_data.original_text:
Situated on the flat summit of a ridge bordering the E side of a steep-sided ravine through which the Ballymeeny River flows. Marked as ‘Saints Grave’ on the 1837 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps and traditionally known as the burial site of St. Farannan. The cairn consists of an oblong, densely-packed heap (L 12m NNE–SSW; 4.8m WNW-ENE; H 1.05m) of small and medium-sized river cobbles. It has a rounded top and broadly slumped sides and is partly moss and sod-covered. At its NE end a modern statue of a saint stands on a concrete pedistal. A low mortared wall (L 4.5m; H 0.6m) of roughly coursed rubble extends S from the E side of the plinth to revet the NE end of the cairn. The cairn is located at the N end of a flat rectangular area (c. 24m N-S; c. 12m E-W) enclosed by a modern iron fence. A rough path leads down the ravine slope to the river. On the E bank of the river is an altar (SL011-058001-).  According to local information, as part of the traditional ‘pattern’, pilgrims visited a holy well (SL011-057----) located c. 60m to NW on the W slope of the ravine. As they returned across the river, they collected a stone from a river pool, also used as a holy well (SL011-058002-) and then placed it on the cairn.

In average to poor pasture, situated on an E-facing slope above the Easky River, which lies 150m to E. Excellent views are afforded in all directions, except at S-SW where they are limited by higher ground. Raised subcircular area (42.2m E-W; 41.7m N-S) enclosed from SSE-N by a largely grass-covered wall of drystone masonry incorporating small quantities of earth. Elsewhere the defining element is a steep scarp faced with massive boulders and stones. No fosse. Original entrance not recognisable. A short distance inside the bank at NW is a small rectangular hut site (SL011-088003-) with an entrance (Wth. 0.6m) in the centre of the N wall. Projecting out from the cashel scarp at SSW is a small square structure (SL011-088004-), possibly an animal shelter. The other three sides of the structure are defined by very wide drystone-built walls (Wth. 2.7m) Only three stones of the wall at the ESE side are still upstanding. There is a possible souterrain (SL011-088002-) in the cashel. The cashel is divided into two approximately equal portions by a NNE-SSW field boundary. Lazy beds traverse the interior.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, situated on level ground at W end of broad SW-NE orientated ridge. A steep N-S orientated W facing slope (H 2m) skirts the external edge of the rath at W. Ground level slopes gently, facing SE immediately to the S of the rath. The rath overlooks slightly lower level ground to the W. Raised roughly circular area (25m E-W; 24m N-S) enclosed by a bank of earth and stone (Wth 7m; int. H 0.35m). A break (Wth 2m) in the bank at SE marks the position of the original entrance. A setting of eight small rubble boulders (av. dims 0.2-0.3m; av. H 0.2m) in an E-W orientated line lies on the NE side of the interior. The centre and SE side of the interior undulate irregularly with many low scarps possibly indicating internal divisions or structures. A modern L-shaped quarry (L E-W stretch 8m; L N-S stretch 6m; Wth top 2m; Wth base 0.5m; D 0.4m) abuts the inner face of the bank at W. Four hut sites (SL011-090002-; SL011-090003-; SL011-090004-; SL011-090005-) are located just outside the perimeter of the rath at E-S, and a fifth hut site (SL011-090006-) is located c. 15m to ESE within a field system (SL011-090007-) that borders the E side of the rath.

Situated in level pasture immediately to the E and SE of, and overlooked by, a rath (SL011-090001). The field system consists of a roughly rectangular area (34m NW-SE; 21m NE-SW) defined by a banks of earth and stone (Wth 1.6m; H 0.4m). The NE side is defined by a low meandering earth and stone bank that links to the bank of Clooneen rath at its NW end and to a roughly N-S orientated field boundary at the SE end. The SE side is defined by a linear scarped edge (H 0.3m). The SW side is defined by a low earth and stone bank. From W-NW, the limit of the system is defined by the bank of the rath. The larger rectangular area is divided by relic boundary consisting of a NE-SW orientated SE facing scarp (L 16.6m; H 0.4m) topped with small rubble boulders extending NE from midway along the SW side of the larger area. At the SE corner of the larger area is a hut site (SL011-090006-) and two smaller fields. The first field is a roughly semi-circular area (10m NW-SE; 10m NE-SW) defined by a low earthen bank (Wth 1.6m; H 0.4m) lying to the W of the hut site. The second field lies to the NE of the hut site and consists of a raised rectangular area (12m NW-SE; 5m NE-SW) defined by an earth and stone bank (Wth 1.6m; int. H 0.3m).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located in the valley of the Easkey River. The castle stands on a slightly elevated, level terrace bordering the W bank of the river. To S, W and NW a strip (Wth c. 40-50m E-W) of soft, boggy ground intervenes between the dry terrace and the low ridge which defines the W side of the valley. The stretch of river immediately to E and SE of the castle is shallow and broken by bedrock terraces and low rocky cataracts, and it is likely that this location was chosen as it provides a natural fording point. This castle is indicated on the 1838 OS-6-inch map as a polygonal enclosure (c. 30-35m E-W; c. 25-30m N-S) named ‘Ballynahowna Castle’. It is not marked on the 1913 edition. The outline of a rectangular building (14.4m N–S; 8.5m E–W) is defined on four sides by slumped, sod-covered stone banks (Wth 3-4m; H 0.6-1.7m) representing collapsed walls. No intact masonry is visible. There is a break (Wth 3m) at the S end of the E side. The stone banks/walls slump broadly into the interior reducing it to an irregular-shaped space (c. 7.4m N–S; 4.8m E–W) with a slightly sunken appearance. Two walls, evident as low, sod-covered wall footings (H 0.2m), extend 5-5.5m to W, one from the NW and one from the SW angles of the rectangular building. They may represent an adjoining room, or another structure or enclosure that abutted the castle. Immediately to SW is the barely discernible outline of a square structure (c. 4.5m N–S; c. 4.5m E–W) which appears to be on the line of a wall, slight remnants of which extends to S for a few meters and then curve to SE before petering out. Low, sod-covered wall footings are also evident c. 25m N of the castle. These slight remains of walls and banks may preserve the outline of a bawn (SL011-092001-) or outer precinct which enclosed the castle but the evidence is meagre and difficult to interpret. 

Compiled by: Jane O’ Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 9 March 2016

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at a possible tower house (SL011-092----) located in the valley of the Easkey River, on a level terrace bordering the W bank of the river. A polygonal enclosure (c. 35m E–W; c. 25m N–S), with a short projection to N at the NE corner, is depicted on the 1837 OS 6-inch map and named ‘Ballynahowna Castle’. It is not shown on the later 25-inch plan or on the 1913 OS 6-inch edition. It may represent a bawn which enclosed a possible tower house (SL011-092----). There is meagre evidence on the ground. The remains of the castle stand on a level, grassy area (Wth c. 40m E–W) bordered to W by damp, boggy ground and at E by a scarp/slope (H c. 2m; Wth c. 4m) which drops to a lower terrace (Wth 5-6m) bordering the river’s edge. Slight remnants of a wall/field boundary, evident as a low, sod-covered rise (Wth 1.5m) define the edge of the grassy area to SW of the castle, and can are also visible c. 25m to N.

Compiled by: Jane O’ Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 9 March 2016

Situated in level wet pasture. Slightly raised roughly square area (21m NW-SE; 20m NE-SW) enclosed by a bank of earth (Wth 2.9m; int. H 0.3m) with a fosse (Wth 3.6m) and an external earthen bank (Wth 3.3m; int. H 0.95m). The original entrance is not recognisable. A modern break (Wth 4m) cuts through the external bank at SW. The external bank is incorporated into a modern, now relic, NE-SW orientated field boundary SE-SW. Co-joined to the NW side of the moated site is an annex consisting of a slightly raised roughly rectangular area (28m NE-SW; 14m NW-SE). The annex is defined by the external bank of the moated site on the SE side and by an earthen bank (Wth 2.65m; int. H 0.4m) at SW-SE. Slight remains of an external fosse (Wth 1.4m) lie outside the bank of the annex at NW-NE. A break (Wth 3m), with a causeway across the fosse, marks the original entrance midway along the NW side. A modern break (Wth 2m) cuts through the bank of the annex at NE. In 2010, in response to forest fires, Sligo County conducted a controlled burn at, and within the vicinity of, the monument. During this operation, part of the enclosing elements of the annex on the NE side and the NE end of the NW side were levelled. A considerable quantity (c. 10m x c. 6m) of displaced stone and earth lies on the internal ground level immediately inside the original circuit of the enclosing elements.

source_data.original_text:
Situated in level wet pasture spanning the S-N flowing Ballymeeny River. Stone bridge (L 7.4m; max. H at centre 1.90m) constructed of roughly quarried limestone blocks bonded with a gravelly limestone mortar. The bridge is supported by three slightly pointed arches evenly spaced across the length of the bridge with the central arch being slightly wider and higher (H 1.5m; Wth 1.45m) while each side arch is smaller (H 1.3m; Wth 1.25m). The arch voussoirs and the key stones are undressed and undifferentiated from the rest of the fabric. The columns (L 1.25m i.e. parallel to water flow; Wth1.15m) on the S side have triangular breakwaters, now partly ruined, of similar fabric to the rest of the bridge. The top of the bridge measures only 1m in width so it is unlikely that walling ever existed.

In pasture, located on a slight E-facing slope, c. 300m SW of the Leaffony River. Very slightly raised, oval area (48m N–S; c. 59.5m E–W) defined by remnants of a partly levelled earthen bank (Wth 1.8m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.4m, at N), truncated at S–SW by an E–W field fence. Another field fence on a NE–SW axis cuts the E–SE edge of the enclosure. Large stones protrude from the bank, some of which, at NW in particular, may be the remnants of stone facing. The interior has a slight slope down from W to E, and the E half appears to be built up somewhat to compensate for this natural slope. In the SE quadrant there is an oblong hollow or pit (max. dim. 8-10m) encircled by a raised rim or bank (W c. 3m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 0.3m) of earth and stones. This appears to be the result of quarrying. There is a souterrain (SL011-135----) 40m to N, and another rath (SL011-085----) located c. 270m to ENE.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 22 April 2013

In rough, wettish pasture, located on a low NW–SE ridge, immediately to S of a rath (SL011-136----) and hut site (SL011-136001-). A subrectangular area (21m NW–SE; 18.4m NE–SW) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.6m, at SE) but open on the NW side. The enclosure has a rather irregular shape. The bank at the N corner, which lies 2m S of the rath, is expanded to a width of c. 5m. The bank on the SE side describes a somewhat meandering line, bowing outwards in a gentle curve. The E corner appears rounded rather than angular. The bank is gapped and poorly preserved on the SE side and also on the SW side, where it may have been incorporated into a field fence on a NW–SE axis. The function of this enclosure, and its relationship to the rath, is unclear. It may be the remnant of a small field plot.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle E-facing slope on the W side of a shallow valley. Exposed in section on the slope is the entrance to a souterrain passage which extends W into the slope. The opening (Wth 0.6m N–S; H 0.35m) is flanked by two upright rounded stones (Wth 0.3-0.35m N–S; H 0.35m) which support a massive lintel boulder (L 1.25m N–S; Wth 0.45m E–W; H 0.48m). The back or W edge of the lintel is partly embedded in the slope but otherwise the lintel is largely exposed and projects from the hill slope. The two side stones extend for 0.5m to W into the passage. Beyond this point, the walls of the passage are constructed of rough drystone walling, 2-3 courses in height, topped with stone lintels. The passage extends W for at least 2m into the body of the slope.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
In an expanse of undulating coastal pasture, bordered at E by the deep-sided ravine of the Ballymeeny River. A relict system of field banks is visible within an area (c. 180m N–S; c. 100m E–W) of undulating terrain bordered at E by the steep-sided ravine of the Ballymeeny River, and at W by a gently dip into a shallow linear depression of damp ground, with a spring/drain that extends to NE to intersect with the ravine. The field banks have been largely levelled and in parts are barely discernible. They appear as low sod-covered linear rises and scarps, with occasional stones protruding from the sod. Some banks appear to define rectilinear areas, but other following natural contours lines. The remains are fragmentary and it is not possible trace a coherent pattern. There is a hut site (SL011-122----), partly enclosed by field banks, roughly in the centre of the field system, and a second hut site (SL011-123----) is located at the NE edge of the area. A rath (SL011-081001-) is located on the SW limits of the field system, an enclosure (SL011-056----) c. 100m to N, and a holy well (SL011-057----) in the ravine to N.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

In the NW corner of a modern walled rectangular field, located in gently undulating coastal grassland, immediately NE of Easkey village. Ground falls very gently for 300m to N ending at a rocky shoreline. The Easkey River lies to E, opening into the sea c. 560m to NE of the enclosure. This enclosure has been partly levelled. It survives as a slightly raised circular area (24.5m N-S; c. 25m E–W) defined at SW–NW by a broadly slumped bank (Wth 4-4.5m) with a relatively pronounced external scarp (ext. H 0.75m). At NNW–S the bank has been levelled and can be traced only as a low curving undulation. Close to the inner edge of the bank in the SW quadrant of the interior there is a circular hollow (5m N–S; c. 4m E–W; D 0.4m) in the centre of which is an upright stone (0.7m ENE-WSW; 0.45-0.5m NNW–SSE; H 0.95m). Abutting the enclosure at SE and S are traces of levelled field boundaries, part of a field system (SL011-143003-) that extend to SE and S. The field boundary at SE appears to connect this enclosure to another enclosure (SL011-143002-) located c. 40m to SE.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 31 December 2013

Located in the N half of a modern walled rectangular field, located in gently undulating coastal grassland. Ground falls very gently for 300m to N ending at a rocky shoreline. The Easkey River lies to E, opening into the sea c. 600m to NE of the enclosure. Subrectangular area (c. 24m NE–SW; c. 15-20m NW–SE) defined by the barely discernible undulations of a levelled bank. The outline of the bank can still be traced in part at S, W and N but is almost entirely obliterated on the E side. The interior is not raised above exterior ground level. Remnants of a levelled field boundary, part of a field system (SL011-143003-), extend to S from the S side of the enclosure. Remnants of another field boundary extend for c. 40m to NW, linking this enclosure to another enclosure (SL011-143001-).

In level, lowlying average pasture. There is a spring well c. 50m to SSE. This enclosure survives as a very low-profile, subrectangular or roughly trapezoidal area (34m E–W; 38m N–S at W, 27m at E) defined on the N, E and S by a slight scarp (H 0.3-0.4m) outside which is a shallow fosse (Wth 2.5-3m; D 0.4m). The enclosing elements are poorly defined but more easily traced on the E and S sides. The enclosure is bordered on the W side by a modern field fence/property boundary flanked by field ditches. Roughly in the centre of the E half of the interior is a shallow oblong depression (9-10m N–S; 6m E-W). Outside the fosse at S is a slightly raised, flat-topped area (Wth 7m N–S) bordered on its S side by a traces of another fosse or field ditch.

source_data.original_text:
This possible promontory fort was first recorded by Casey (1999, 89-90). It consists of a truncated headland evident as a small, roughly triangular grass-covered area (c. 8m E–W; c. 3-3.5m N–S) jutting N from the E–W cliff face. The triangular projection has a raised S-sloping surface, interpreted by Casey as remnants of an inner bank. On its landward edge, it is defined by remnants of a fosse with an external bank. The fosse (Wth 1.6-1.8m, Wth base c. 1m) is evident as a shallow depression, and the external bank (W 1.8-2m) is barely discernible as a slight rise, dropping 0.3-0.4m into the fosse on its inner edge, and almost flush with surrounding field level on its outer edge. Roughly mid-way along the fosse there is a causeway (Wth 1.8m). The fosse and external bank curve in a long, shallow arc (L c. 15-16m) ending at the cliff edge on either side of the triangular projection. A post and wire fence extends along the inner edge of the fosse. The interior area of the possible promontory fort has been almost entirely eroded away. However, a projecting, roughly triangular-shaped ledge (c. 10m E–W, c. 3-4m N–S) of rock, 3m below the cliff top, gives an indication of the original size and shape of the headland.

source_data.original_text:
FtzPatrick (2007, 11) stated that 'over 200 earthen enclosures dotting the 'ruans' or commons on the cliff line of the headland are not of great antiquity but modern platforms for stacking harvested dry sea wrack. The wrack was stacked in small cocks and remained there until it was carried away and burnt with sea rods to make kelp, or spread on the land as manure. The results of an excavation (01E0700), combined with analysis of aerial photographs, local lore, nineteenth-century estate documents and eighteenth-century travellers' observations, indicate that many of the enclosures are likely to date from the modern period and are primarily related to tenant activity on the estates of Cooper of Markree and Hillas of Donecoy in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The harvesting of sea wrack for the iodine market and for local potato and grain crops continued at Aughris on a small scale into the first half of the twentieth century.' The example excavated by E. FitzPatrick in 2001 is located at the following grid reference (ITM): 549055 (easting), 836022 (northing).
 
FitzPatrick, E., with contributions by Fenwick J. (2007), 'Interpreting a cultural landscape: a case for sea-weed harvesting at Aughris, Co. Sligo' JIA, 11-34.

FitzPatrick, E. (2001) 'The gathering place of Tír Fhiachragh: archaeological and folkloric investigations at Aughris, Co. Sligo' PRIA 101C, 67-105.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, encompassing the highest point on a ridge-top plateau. When approached from S the elevated position is not appreciated, however at N−NE there is a steep fall of ground, which then levels out somewhat to a more gradual slope extending to the rocky coastline 800m away. The location provides extensive views along a strip of coastal pasture, the shoreline and out to sea. Knocknarae is visible to E and the Ox Mountains form the skyline to S.
Oval area (126.8m N–S; 111.2m E–W) defined by a broad, flat-based fosse (Wth 5m at top, 2.8m at base; int. D 1.75m, at S) with a substantial external bank (Wth 6.4-6.8m; int. H 2m; ext. H 1.35m, at S). Stone facing is evident on the inner face of the bank at N–NE and W-NW, but this may be relatively modern in date. The original entrance may be at the SE where there is a causeway (Wth 2m) across the fosse, with a corresponding gap in the external bank, now blocked by a low modern field bank. At the S, another section (Wth 4.6m) of the fosse has been partly infilled to form a shallow causeway, leading to two breaks (Wth 1m) in the external bank, separated by a remnant of a field bank that extends to S. The W half of the interior is relatively level, but the E half slopes down from W to E, reflecting the natural ridge slope. Located slightly off-centre to NE within the interior, straddling the slope described above, there is a smaller enclosure (SL012-008002-), now partly levelled. This second enclosure (diam. 61.6m N–S; 52m E–W) occupies much of the internal space in the centre of the larger hilltop enclosure, leaving a clear space of c. 25-30m between it and the enclosing fosse of the larger enclosure. 
In the NW quadrant of the hilltop enclosure, there is a Napoleonic Era stone-built signal tower (SL012-008003-). A field fence, on a roughly E–W axis, cuts through the N half of the both the hilltop enclosure and the smaller enclosure.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 1 April 2015

source_data.original_text:
Situated on flat ground with a steep curving slope to the N which drops down to the coastal plain, (83m OD). The surrounding area consists of enclosed pasture defined by stone walls. It is located within a large circular enclosure of possible Neolithic date (Kelly 2018) that consists of an external ditch and an internal bank (SL012-008001-). A mortared rubble stone wall runs from E to W across the enclosure, dividing off the signal tower and the northern third of the enclosure from the southern two thirds. The wall was an element of the enclosed landscape in which the signal tower is set. Within the large enclosure there is a smaller sub-circular ditched enclosure (SL012-008002-) suspected to be an early medieval enclosure. The site has unobstructed views in all directions. Rathlee Signal Tower (SL011-025001-), located c. 10.6kms to the WNW, is currently obscured by intervening forestry. Knocklane Hill Signal Tower SL007-057----), located c. 16.6kms to the NE, has been largely demolished\collapsed and cannot be seen from the site. 

An early nineteenth-century (c. 1804-6) two-storey square-plan signal tower, built with roughly coursed rubble stone masonry (int. dims. 4.31m N-S x 4.52m E-W)). The signal tower is particularly well preserved, surviving to its full height (H. c. 11.25). The N wall is the tallest with the other sides being slightly lower, reflecting the slight slopes\topography of the area adjacent to the tower. The N wall features a square-headed doorway to the centre at first floor level that would have been accessed via a retractable ladder. The doorway retains cut stone block-and-start surrounds, cut stone threshold, and cut stone lintel over with central projecting keystone. The door is protected by a wide machicolation over supported by three sloping cut stone corbels with two cut stone slabs providing the base at parapet level. The machicolation features short narrow gun loops in the centre of each of its three walls. The E and W walls each feature two square-headed windows at ground and first floor levels. The N ground floor window on the E wall was later opened up to form a ground floor entrance. Cut stone block-and-start surrounds, cut stone sills, and cut stone lintels with projecting keystones are retained to all window openings apart from the window opening later widened to create a doorway. The first floor windows on both the E and W walls have been blocked up with neat rubble stone masonry. The S wall features a central slight outward bulge that houses the chimney flue. A partially collapsed rubble stone chimneystack is located on top of the centre of the S elevation. A small horizontal chute passes through the E side of the S wall at ground level, connecting to the top of the semi-basement level. The SE and SW corners of the signal tower are protected by bartizans supported by three sloping cut stone corbels, with two large stone slabs providing the base of each bartizan at parapet level. The bartizans project straight out from the wall and feature sharp curving corners on the diagonal points. The bartizans feature short narrow gun loops in the centre of each of their four walls. The parapet survives to all elevations, which extends around the bartizans and the machicolation over the door, and retains fine chamfered cut stone coping over. 

The internal space consists of a semi-basement level, which is almost entirely infilled with soil, a ground-floor room with a split mezzanine level, a first-floor room, and a low attic level. The flat roof had been accessible from the attic level. The floors and the roof of the building had been wooden and were carried in the thickness of the wall. No parts of the floors or the roof have survived but rows of joist-holes indicate their former positions. The internal walls are covered in a layer of smooth lime render, although this does not extend into the semi-basement level. The S wall features central fireplaces flanked by segmental-headed alcoves at the ground floor and by square-headed alcoves at first floor level. The chute which passes through the S wall opened up into the semi-basement level below the position of the E ground floor alcove. A square sectioned internal drainage channel runs down the SE corner of the building. This is believed to have brought rainwater from the roof to storage barrels in the semi-basement.

The signal tower was part of a system of over 80 signal stations constructed by the British Board of Ordnance in the first decade of the 19th century to warn of the approach of a French invasion fleet. Signalling between sites was accomplished using a naval signal post. The system formed a continuous chain from Dublin Bay running clockwise all the way around the coast to Malin Head in County Donegal. It was abandoned by the mid-1810s when the threat of a French invasion diminished (Kerrigan 1995, 157-66).

source_data.original_text:
Long, narrow, triangular promontory (dims. 55m N-S; 16m E-W) extending N into Sligo Bay. Its W, N and E sides are defined by low cliffs upon a rocky shelf while it is cut off from the surrounding land by a largely levelled, low bank of earth and stone (Wth. 1m; H 0.6m) at S. A short distance S of this is a second bank which has been levelled but whose outline is still identifiable (Wth. c.1.5m). The promontory is marked 'Donaghintraine' on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map. O'Rorke (1890, 403) recorded that this is an anglisization of 'Dun Contreathain' or 'Dun Cintreathain' and that there was a great battle at a fortress here in 1249 between Felim O'Conor and the Berminghams at which O'Conor emerged victorious. (O'Rorke 1878, 256-7; M. Casey 1988, pers. comm.)

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a headland defined by rock cliffs which drop to a stone beach and a rocky shoreline. A stream, flowing N in a narrow gully, bisects the headland to E of centre. Toward the N end of the headland, the stream flows through a deeper rock-faced ravine, which has been partly expanded by quarrying on it W side. Another stream borders the W side of the headland, and a modern road, leading to a pier, lies immediately to W of the headland. A disused, grassed-over trackway, bordered by field banks, extends E–W across the S side of the headland. Evidence of the promontory fort is located on the E part of the headland, bordered by the stream gully at W and by the natural cliff at NNW–E. The landward side of the promontory is cut off by two low-profile banks with external fosses. The innermost bank (Wth c. 2m; H 0.4m) is very low, though somewhat higher and more clearly defined at its W end. Intervening between it and the outer bank is a fosse (Wth c. 3m). The outer bank (Wth 3.5-4m; H 0.5m) is broadly slumped. It is bordered externally by the outermost fosse (Wth 3-3.5m). The enclosed area forms a somewhat irregular-shaped oblong measuring c. 25-30m N–S by c. 20-25m E–W. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 6 March 2014

source_data.original_text:
Situated in lowlying, poorly-drained pasture, within a graveyard (SL012-025002-). The OS Letters (1836, 310 (127-8)) recorded that 'Templeboy' is an anglicization of 'Teampall Buidhe', 'the church of St. Baothain' who was the patron saint of the parish. Late medieval church (ext. dims. 19.3m E-W; 7.15m N-S - Wall T 0.74m) incorporating the W wall of an earlier church. The E wall has a slight external base batter. Slightly off-centre in the E wall is a tall ogee-headed, lancet window. The W wall is constructed of large blocks, typical of the early medieval period. It contains a blocked-up lintelled doorway. This type of masonry is also present in the W end of the N wall. Close to the W end of the N wall is an internally recessed doorway. The S wall is poorly preserved and is apparently featureless. O'Rorke (1889, 404-5) recorded a holy well (SL012-025006-) dedicated to St. Molaisse, located close to the church. 

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the outskirts of Dromore West village, situated on a low rise on a high bluff overlooking a bend in the River Dunneill. A castle, named ‘Dooniell Castle’ is shown at this location on the Down Survey (1655-6) map. It is marked 'Site of Dunneill Castle' on the 1837 OS 6-inch map. It was an O'Dowd castle and took its name from Neill, a chieftain of the family. It later fell into the hands of the MacSweeneys. In 1641, according to some depositions, the castle was in the charge of 'Gullne duff O'Hart of Carbury' (Kilgannon 1926, 297-8; ITA Survey 1942-4). Subcircular mound (c.30m NE-SW; c.25m NW-SE; H 1.7m at NW; 3m at SE) of earth and stone, which shows considerable evidence of past quarrying and disturbance. There is no masonry visible.

In pasture, situated on a NE-SW ridge, at the break of slope on the N side where ground falls away quite steeply. Slightly raised oval area (47m N-S; 38m E-W) defined at E by a remnant of an earthen bank (Wth 1.7m; H 0.3m) which has been levelled elsewhere to a scarp (H 0.8m at W). In the S half of the rath is a souterrain (SL012-078003-). In the NW quadrant is a possible hut site (SL012-078002-). A modern field fence, on a NE-SW axis, cuts the E–SE edge of the rath. A low N–S relict field bank (Wth 2.1m) lies 2m to W of the rath. It extends c. 30m beyond the rath to S then curves to NE.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a low hillock or terrace on a general N-facing slope, in sharply undulating terrain. There is a stream c. 30m to E. Knocknarae is visible to E. This enclosure consists of a roughly circular area (diam. c. 16-18m) defined by a low, degraded bank (Wth c. 4-5m; int. H 0.1m; ext. H 0.4-0.7m) which is faced internal and externally with a kerb of large stones. The bank is evident SE–NW as a broad stony rise but at N-NE its original line can be traced only as a shallow arc of large upright stones and boulders, which appears to represent the remains of the bank kerb. Dense overgrowth obscures the bank at E-S. At W, a setting of large upright stones defines an entrance way through the enclosing bank. The entrance is flanked at its innermost end by a matching pair of large, upright stone slabs, and is c. 1.20 in width. Towards the exterior of the bank, the entrance appears to widen or splay outwards and is faced by a setting of smaller upright stones. In the SE quadrant, there is a possible house (SL012-095004-), roughly rectangular in plan. The remnant of a later field bank, on a roughly NW–SE axis, lies adjacent to the NE side of the enclosure, and close to the S side of the enclosure, there is an isolated remnant of a E-W field wall, engulfed in overgrowth. It was recorded as a stone fort by Ó Nualláin (1989, 95, Appendix: no. 3). There is a rath (SL012-094----) located c. 65m to SW, and a possible passage tomb (SL012-0127----) located c. 140m downslope to N.

In pasture, situated a short distance above the rocky shoreline at Aughris Head. Not marked on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. When inspected in 1993 this holy well consisted of a natural spring flowing from beneath a scarped slope where the field borders the shoreline. Since that date, the spring has been enclosed by stone slabs to create a small pool or well. Adjacent to the spring, a modern drystone wall (L 3m; H 1.7m), constructed of stone slabs, has been built against the scarp, enclosing a slab-lined altar (L 1.55m; W 0.7m) on which stands a small modern statue of the Virgin Mary.  Immediately to E of this is a 'prayer cairn' of small stones. According to local tradition, the well is dedicated to St. Patrick. The whole complex is enclosed by a post and wire fence.

In pasture, located on the level top of a ridge with a gentle fall of ground to E. This rath has been greatly modified. Only the enclosing elements on the W half of the rath (diam. c. 20-25m) survive, incorporated into the W side of a roughly square field plot (c. 25m N–E; c. 25m E-W). The extant remains consist of an earthen bank (Wth 4.4m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 1.4m) with an external fosse (3-3.5m) and external bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 1.1m; ext. H 0.7m) which curve SW–NW in a shallow arc. The interior of the rath appears to have been subsumed into the field plot, and the banks and fosse at NNW–SSSW have been levelled and replaced by the linear field banks which define the N, E, and S sides of the square field. Abutting the E side of the field, at its N end, are the sod-covered stone foundations (10m N–S; 4m E–W) of a rectangular vernacular house (SL012-115002-). A slightly sunken, grass-covered track way extend from the house downslope to ENE.

source_data.original_text:
Situated in a shallow valley into which a stream feeds from the S and forms a large pool to the SW of the monument. The ground rises to the S and N and there are limited views from the monument to E and W. The remains consist of a sub-circular cairn (c. 17.50m NNE-SSW and c. 21m WNW-ESE; averaging between 0.7m and 1m high) which is delimted by a kerb of boulders, seventeen of which appear to be in situ with many others displaced around the perimeter. The kerb is absent along the NW side and there is a gap in it at the E. The interior is composed of small stones which are covered with a thin layer of soil and vegetation. A raised bank-like feature runs N-S tangential to the cairn on its W side and incorporates a number of the kerb-stones. It expands at each end into a mound-like terminal: that on the S appears as an extension of the cairn. The precise nature of this feature is unclear as is its relationship to the cairn. The remains have clear affinities with the boulder-circle monuments within the Carrowmore passage-tomb cemetery and interpretation as a possible example of this class would not be inconsistent with the present evidence. This, however, is purely tentative and a proper elucidation of the monument must await further investigation. (Timoney 2015)

Situated on a low rise in poor pasture. Raised circular platform (diam. 28m) atop a very high, steep-sided mound of earth and stone (H 5m). The platform is enclosed by a bank of earth and stone (Wth. 2m; int. H 0.55m - 0.9m). Between the outer foot of the bank and the edge of the platform is a narrow berm (Wth. 1.5m - 2.5m). Outer bank has been incorporated into a NE-SW field boundary from NNE-E-ESE. At SSE is a ramped causeway which extends from the wide entrance gap (Wth. 4m) across the fosse. The internal area slopes appreciably from W-E. Tradition of a souterrain at this site (see SL013-009002-). A short distance W is the remains of a disused field system (see SL013-009003-).

In pasture, situated on level summit of a prominent knoll, named Sheeanmore Hill, with extensive views in all directions. Knocknarae, crowned by Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-) dominates the view to E, the Ox Mountains define the horizon at S, and the broad sweep of Sligo Bay is visible to N. A children's burial ground (SL013-012003-) is located downslope to W, and field banks of a later field system (SL013-012004-) traverse the hill slopes.

Situated on lower S facing slopes of Sheeanmore Hill in pasture. Roughly rectangular area (dims 14m E-W; 13m N-S) enclosed by a bank of earth and stone (Wth 2.2m-4m; int. H 0.3m-0.5m; ext. H 0.2m-0.3m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. Probable entrance feature is marked by a pair of upright rectangular slabs, standing 0.4m apart, extending perpendicularly from the inner face of the bank at N (W stone-T 0.3m; H 1m; E stone- T 0.2m; H .4m). The interior of the site is strewn with rubble limestone that is concentrated into thirteen low cairns (av. dims. Wth base 2m; H 0.3m) There are also five roughly rectangular quarried limestone blocks (L 0.6m-1m; 0.25m-0.35m square) strewn in no clear order. Site is known locally as an infants' burial ground.

source_data.original_text:
On a slight rise in good, rough pasture, E of Ardnaglass bridge and N of the main Ballysadare-Easky road with excellent views. Named 'Ardnaglass Castle' on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. Apparently built by the O'Dowds, the Lords of Tireragh. Rectangular castle, (int. dims. c. 32m NW-SE; 21m W-E) aligned NW-SE of which only the SE wall (L 15.3m; H 8-10m) and a corner portion of the NW wall survive. The SE wall has a neatly angular corner champfer on the SW end and on the W end of the wall framing the corner is a solid machicolation projection supported by massy brackets, with an intact gun loop at W. The walls are slightly battered (T 1.35m), the basal plinth acting as a supporting buttress and have an ashlar finish covering a fabric of random rubble and lime mortar. Over the plinth batter is a central window with ashlar surround with a gun loop to E. The ground rises to the NE where the sod-covered remains of the wall may indicate the remains of a bastion-type entrance. The N corner of the NW wall survives, with precisely cut quoins and a similar machicolated projection facing N. To the W are a series of earthworks (SL013-048002-), to the S is a house site (SL013-048003-), to SW is a moated site (SL013-048005-). The castle was the original location of a stone sculpture (DU018-221---- ) which is now in the National Museum of Ireland . It consists of a bas-relief of two intertwined animals, interpreted as a dog killing a wolf (Wood-Martin 1882, 57, fig. 5A; Kilgannon 1926, 293; 292-3).

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located to W of an Anglo-Norman castle (SL013-048001-) and to N of a moated site (MA013-048005-). A N-S bye-road intervenes between the earthworks and the castle.
Listed in the RMP (1995) as ‘earthworks’ based on features visible in an aerial photograph (ACP V203/66-5, roll 128, pr. 25). The earthworks cover an area of c. 120m N−S by c. 65m E−W in the E part of a modern rectangular walled field, bordered on the E side by the road. The earthworks are not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps, but this part of the field is indicated as ‘Fair Green’ on the 3rd edition OS 6-inch map. 
In aerial view, the earthworks consist of a series of linear undulations outlining a patchwork of small subrectangular spaces (max. dims. 20-30m). The NE−SW alignment of the plots runs counter to the predominantly N−S/E−S layout of the present-day field system. The remains may represent house or garden plots, possibly associated with settlement which grew up around the castle in the medieval or post-medieval period. The remains are indistinct and difficult to trace at ground level.

Compiled by: Jane 0'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 19 June 2020

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, this enclosure straddles an E-W orientated ridge, which provides excellent views in all directions. Oval area (c. 75m N-S; 68m E-W) defined by an earthen scarped edge (ext. H 1.5m at W, 0.3m at NE), and enclosed by a fosse (Wth top 6.6m) with an external earthen bank (Wth base 4.75m; int. H 2.9m; ext. H 1.3m at W).
Along the NE and SW arcs, the scarp is low and degraded, the fosse largely infilled and the outer bank levelled to a low rise. The interior of the site is not artificially raised, but follows the natural slopes of the ridge so that the centre, W and E are flush with external ground level, but the N and S sides are higher (by c. 2.5m) than external ground level. The location of the original entrance is uncertain; a causeway (Wth 4m) across the fosse at NW appears to be modern, allowing access to a now disused rectangular quarry pit (c. 20m N-S; c. 10m E-W; D 2m), which cuts through the scarp at N and extends S into the interior. A smaller oval quarry pit (6m N-S; 4m E-W; D 1.5m) cuts across the scarp at NNW. A NNE-SSW drystone field wall extends through the enclosure to E of centre. A rath (SL013-063001-) and an enclosure(SL013-063002-) are located 90m to NW, and there is another rath (SL013-062----) 160m to N.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of revised upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Situated on the summit of a ridge adjacent to the shore of the Finne Estuary in Ballysadare Bay. Raised D-shaped area (dims. 22.7m NE-SW; 9.8m NW-SE) atop a high, steep-sided mound of earth and stone. From NE-E-SSW this is defined by a severely eroded, linear cliff face. Elsewhere the defining element is a scarp (H 3.4m - 3.6m) which has a low bank of earth and stone at its upper edge from SSW-SW-WSW. At the foot of the scarp and bank from SSW-SW-WSW and from NNW-N-NE is a very wide, steep-sided, flat-bottomed fosse (Wth. 11.5m - 12m; D 2m). Original entrance not recognisable. The evidence suggests that the extant remains represents the NW third of a small raised rath, the remainder of which has been eroded away.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

In pasture, at the SE tip of Ballinlig point, a narrow finger of land that juts into the W end of Ballysadare Bay, and overlooks a small river estuary to S. A layer (L c. 8m NE–SW; D 0.3m) of shells in a matrix of dark brown soil is exposed in section, immediately below the sod line, on the eroding E end of the peninsula. The midden has accumulated against the S-facing slope of a ridge and may extend beneath the sod for c. 6m to W of the exposed section. It is composed of a dense concentration of oyster shells, with a few periwinkles and cockle shells also visible. There is a hut site (SL013-087003-) c. 7m to W and another hut site (SL013-087003-) c. 10m to SW. There is another midden (SL013-087002-) located c. 80m to NW.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Situated on slight N-facing slope in gently undulating pasture to the N of Sheeanmore Hill. Field system is shown on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map as a series of curving field boundaries. Two elements of the field system are most prominent. The first is a relic N-S orientated gently meandering boundary (L c. 250m) consisting of an earth and stone bank (Wth 3.2m; H 0.3m-0.5m) with a slight fosse/drain (Wth 0.5m; D 0.3m) on the E side. At the S end of this boundary, a series of E-W orientated boundaries are indicated on the OS 6-inch map but these have been levelled and are not visible at ground level. The second prominent element is a curving E-W orientated boundary (L 60m) linking to the W side of the main N-S boundary consisting of a relic low earthen bank (Wth 2.5m; H 0.3m) that lies on the top of a slight N facing natural scarp. The field system extends south into the archaeological complex on Sheeanmore hill (SL013:012002-; SL013-012003- and SL013-012004-).

Located in improved pasture/silage, on a gentle S-facing slope. A possible souterrain was noted here in November 2003. The visible remains consisted of a horizontally-set slab (L c. 0.8m; T c. 0.1-0.5m) which protruded slightly from the natural slope. The slab had the appearance of a roof lintel and overlay a cavity or possible passage (Wth c. 1m; H at least 0.65m) lined with drystone walling, which appeared to extend into the hill slope. The structure was largely infilled with soil; it was not possible to determine its original dimensions or orientation. An inspection in 2014 found that reclamation works had taken place in the field and there is no surface trace of the possible souterrain.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a low, level elevation in gently undulating terrain. Immediately to N the ground falls away, giving excellent views to NE across Ballysadare Bay, prominently framed by Ben Bulben and Knocknarae. Ground rises very gradually to S. This circular enclosure (diam. c. 64m) is defined by a levelled scarp, probably originally a bank, which has been modified or truncated by linear field boundaries at SW and NW. The eastern arc of the enclosure can be traced at N−SSW as low, grass-covered undulation/scarp (ext. H 0.3-0.55m). Two large boulders (max. dim. c. 2m)lie on the line of the undulation at NE. The western arc of the enclosure has been modified: At SSW−W it is defined by a linear, sod-covered bank (Wth 1.6-2m), with a pronounced inward-facing scarp (H 0.6-0.8m) incorporating large stones and boulders. This bank may be a remnant of the original enclosing bank, but its linear nature suggests modification in the modern era to serve as a field boundary. At NW the enclosing bank is truncated by a NE−SW drystone field wall which coincides with the townland boundary between Fallathurteen and Carrrowreagh. This field wall is linear in form, except for a short section at NNW which respects the curve of the enclosure. The enclosing scarp/undulation is lowest at E, possibly the site of the original entrance. There is a gentle drop in ground level in the SE quadrant bordered by a low broadly sloping scarp. A drystone field wall, on a WNW−ESE axis, bisects the interior to NE of centre. Relict cultivation ridges are visible in the interior and in the surrounding fields. There is a wedge tomb (SL013-028----) 335m to NE, a castle (SL013-029002-) and bawn (SL013-029003-) incorporated into a rath (SL013-029001-) 300m to ENE, and another enclosure (SL013-030----) 275m to E.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 9 December 2016

source_data.original_text:
Situated at a cliff edge c. 15m above sea level, overlooking Kilalla Bay. D-shaped raised area (70m NE-SW; 45m NW-SE). Its straight side, from SW-NNW, is defined by the steep sea cliff. The remainder is enclosed by four banks of earth and stone with external fosses. The innermost bank (Wth 8m; int. H 0.8m) and fosse (Wth 11.4m; D 3.2m) are the most substantial. At the outer edge of the fosse are two less substantial banks and fosses. At the outer edge of the 3rd fosse is a berm (Wth 2.5-3m). Beyond this are the fourth and least sunstantial bank (Wth 3.5m; H 0.5m) and fosse (Wth 2.4m; D 0.6-0.9m). A stone-lined break (Wth 2.4m) in the inner bank at S, with a causeway across inner fosse and corresponding breaks in the other banks, represents the original entrance. A series of large flat slabs extend from the entrance to the centre of the enclosed area. From there they curve off in a W direction ending at the cliff edge. Their purpose appears to be to separate the SW quadrant, which is raised 0.5m - 0.7m, from the remainder. Within the SW quadrant are the fragmentary remains of three circular hut sites (SL016-001002-; SL016-001003-; SL013-001004-). One is located only 2m back from the cliff edge. In the SE quadrant are the remains of a possible fourth hut site (SL016-001005-). Remains of a possible souterrain (SL SL016-0010006-) are visible in section in the cliff face at the NW edge of the enclosure. A series of disused field boundaries and enclosures (SL016-001007-) are located 30m to N. The enclosure is named 'Cahermore' on the 1913 OS 6-inch map, and is traditionally associated with the O'Caoimhin family.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
On a low rise in pasture, located at the N end of a subrectangular, walled graveyard (SL016-011002-). Traditionally believed to be the site of an early monastery founded by St. Molaisse (local information). The present remains are of a late 16th century parish church (20.9m E-W; 7.35m N-S; Wall T 0.85m), whose walls survive to full height. Large, almost flat-headed window in E wall. At the W end of the S wall is doorway with rear flat segmental arch and external pointed two-centered arch, and three windows with almost flat-headed segmental arches. Close to the E end of this wall is a single slit ope with rear splay while at the E end proper is a large rectangular recess, probably a piscina. At the W end of the N wall is a window with an almost flat-headed segmental arch. The E end of this wall has a heavy covering of ivy. Nonetheless two blocked-up opes are visible. There is evidence for a second storey, probably a priest's residence, over the W end. Within the church is the tomb (SL016-011004-) of James Wood d. 1692 which was restored by a relative in 1861. 

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Situated a short distance NE of Enniscrone village. Early 17th century rectangular fortified house (c. 14m E-W; 8.05m N-S ; Wall T 0.95m) constructed upon a artifically constructed subrectangular platform (c. 50m E-W; c. 30m N-S; H 1.5-1.8m) on a naturally-occurring E-W ridge. The structure is two storeys in height with attics. There are identical, circular projecting towers (diam. 4.25m; Wall T 0.63) at the NW and SW angles. An early 19th century plan of the site (OS Letters 1836, 292 (118-9)) shows projecting, circular towers at the remaining angles but these, the E wall and the E end of the S wall have since been destroyed. The entrance (Wth 1.35m), with drawbar sockets still intact, is in the centre of the N wall. On either side of the entrance are plain, rectangular, flat-headed windows. At ground floor level in the S wall are 3 similar windows. Only the W portion of that at the E end has survived. At first floor level in the N and S walls, above those at ground floor level, are similar windows. In the W wall, which contains a massive chimney with a rectangular base, there are large fireplaces at ground and first floor levels. That at ground floor level has a small oven built into its S side. Both surviving towers contain three small, rectangular flat-headed windows and four narrow gun loops at both ground and first floor levels.
The original castle, of which there are no remains surviving, was constructed in 1560 by the Mhic Fhirbhisigh family which supplied hereditary poets and historians to the O'Dowds of Tireragh (Killanin and Duignan 1989 ed., 205). In 1597 Fearadach and Cormac MacDonnell sold it to John Crofton. Crofton subsequently sold it to Thomas Nolan of Ballinrobe whose son was living there in 1642. In 1641 it was commandeered and garrisioned by the Irish. In 1642 it was the scene of a skirmish between the crown forces and a local militia. In 1645 it was captured by the Cromwellian army. After the end of the war it became the property of Sir Thomas Gore. (O'Rorke 1890, 418; Kilgannon 1926, 303; ITA Survey 1942-4; Jope 1961, 271-2; Highwood Community Resource Centre 1998, 36)

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

Situated in level pasture, a short distance W of a N-S ridge. Situated atop a low ridge in pasture. Circular, steep-sided mound of earth and stone (diam. at base c. 2 1m; H 2.8m). At the top of the mound is a small irregularly-shaped, almost level area (dims. 5.1m NNE-SSW; 4.2m WNW-ESE). The mound is encircled by a wide, deep fosse (Wth 3.8m) which has a substantial bank of earth and stone (Wth. 6.5m; max. H 1m) at its outer lip. On the OS 1912 edition of the OS 25-inch map are five irregularly-shaped, recumbent boulders with the collective designation 'Standing Stones (Called the Children of the Mermaid)'. A sixth was identified during the site visit. A seventh is recorded in a legend, much of which is based at the site, which was recorded by Wood-Martin (1887-8, 290). There is no evidence that any of the boulders were ever in an upright position.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on the NE side of a low ridge in undulating pasture. Wood-Martin (1882, 113-4) recorded a 'subterranean chamber, with several smaller chambers off'. Two adjacent passages have been identified. Both are walled with drystone masonry and roofed with massive lintels. The first (visible L 5-6m; Wth 1.25m; H 0.8m) is aligned E-W and appears to terminate at a wall at its E end. At its W end, at surface level, an area of surface subsidence (L c. 6m N-S; Wth 2.4m) hints that a subsidary passage may extending N at right angles from the main passage. The second passage, which is located a short distance E of the first, is also aligned E-W. At its E end is an area of collapse (L 2m E-W) which opens into a small passage (L c. 3m E-W; Wth c. 1m) that terminates at a stone wall at its W end. There is no obvious link between the two passages but, given their proximity and alignment, it is probable that they are part of the same structure.

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Not marked on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. Situated near the S edge of the top of a steep-sided ridge. Souterrain, whose walls are constructed of slightly corbelled drystone masonry and which is roofed with stone lintels. Present entrance is an opening (Wth 0.6m; H 0.4m) topped with a stone lintel, located 1m below ground surface on the E side of a quarried area (8m N-S; 6m E-W). This gives access to a narrow pasage (Wth 0.6-1m; H 1.1m; L 4.8m) which inclines downwards in an E direction. At ground floor level in the N wall at the E end of the passage is a small, partially blocked-up recess (Wth 0.61m; H 0.57m). The passage ends at a lintelled doorway (Wth 0.67m; H 1.05m) which open onto a oval-shaped chamber (dims. 4m x 2.5m; H 2.45m). At SW, 1m above present floor level, is a small, semi-circular recess or cupboard. At the SE is a short passage (L 1.8m N-S; Wth 0.6m; H 1.05m) which gives access to a second roughly oval-shaped chamber (L 3.8m N-S; Wth 1.8m; H c. 2m). At NE is a small recess or cupboard. There is a local tradition of a rath in proximity to this site (SL016-070----).
