source_data.original_text:
At the W edge of a pasture field, located in an eroding cliff face (H 1.5m) above a storm beach. This slab-lined burial was partly eroded from the cliff face and a rescue excavation was carried out by the OPW in 1991 (Buckley et al. 1991-2). The grave, which underlay topsoil (D 0.3m), was cut into a layer (D 0.5m) of shingle which overlay limestone bedrock. It was oriented roughly E-W, with the head to the W, but by the time of the excavation the W end was already destroyed by erosion. The E end (1m E–W; 0.5m N–S) remained intact. The sides of the grave were constructed of limestone slabs set on edge with chocking stones in between. Two overlapping sets of flat slabs formed the roof. The poorly preserved leg bones of an adult, or more probably a sub-adult, individual were recovered. The slab walls of the grave, which were left in situ when the excavation was completed, have since been eroded by wave action. A slight subsidence (Wth 1m N-S) at the cliff edge is all that now marks the location. In local tradition the grave was known as the ‘Fisherman’s Grave’.

Date of upload: 2 September 2013

When noted in 1991 it was interpreted as a barrow, however, it appears to have been very similar in form and size to kelp-drying kilns (See for instance SL012-002001-) found elsewhere along the west Sligo coastline. On the SE margins of Enniscrone village, located in an expanse of damp, rush-grown pasture in the flat valley bottom of the Bellawaddy River. The field is bordered c. 100m to N of the mound by the river which opens into the sea c. 300m to NW. The E, S and W sides of the field are bordered by land drains. A roughly circular rise (c. 22m E–W; c. 23m N–S; H 1.7m at N, 1.5m at S) with a flattened top (c. 8m N–S, c. 8m E–W) and broadly sloping sides (Wth slope c. 9m). The sides have a somewhat more elongated slope to NW and SE, which gives the mound the appearance of being more oval than circular. It is likely that prior to the digging of the modern system of drainage ditches, this area constituted very wet land. It is possible that the mound represents the remains of some form of wetland habitation site or crannog.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a level terrace on a ridge, with a gentle slope c. 10m to NW and a marked fall of ground into the small valley of the Devlin River which is 240m to W. Two raths (SL016-056----; SL016-055001-) are located 170m to E and 150m to SW, respectively.
This stone-lined grave was discovered in June 2021 at a depth of 0.4-0.5m below surface by the landowner while digging a trench to take a narrow-bore plastic water pipe for connection to water troughs. The ground works disturbed the W end of the grave, displacing some of the stones and exposing human bones.
The discovery was notified immediately to the National Monuments Service (NMS) and the National Museum of Ireland (NMI), and a rescue excavation (21E0643) was undertaken by NMI in September 2021 (Seaver 2022).
The excavation revealed a lintelled grave (L 2.1m; Wth 0.5m; D 0.3m) containing the extended skeleton of an adult individual, oriented roughly E−W, with the head at W. The floor of the grave was unlined, the bones lying directly on the soil. The long sides were constructed of contiguous and overlapping upright slabs, and the head and foot of the grave was defined by naturally occurring stones/bedrock. It was roofed by a row of overlapping, horizontally-laid slabs/lintels. It was necessary to dismantle the grave in the process of excavation, but some of the side slabs remain in situ, and the grave was backfilled when the excavation was completed.
Post-excavation analysis included specialist examination of the skeletal remains (L. Lynch, in Seaver 2022) and radiocarbon dating of a sample of bone. The radiocarbon determination returned a date of Cal AD 403-538 (UBA-46950, 2δ) placing the burial in the earliest phase of the Early Medieval period. Osteological analysis established that the burial was of an adult male, aged between 35 and 45 years at time of death. His estimated height of 172.6cm [c. 5 ft 7 inches] is relatively tall for men of this period, and an indication of good nutrition in childhood. His teeth exhibit severe deposits of calcified plaque, and the heavy wear on the crowns is evidence of a coarse diet, usual in this period. Chipping of the enamel most likely relates to the coarse diet, rather than to occupational use of the teeth. There is evidence of mild degenerative joint disease in bones on his right-hand side.
The absence of skeletal signs of childhood physiological stress, his relatively tall stature and low levels of joint wear suggest that during his life he benefitted from adequate nutrition and was possibly somewhat sheltered from prolonged, heavy physical work. This, combined with the care taken in the construction of the grave, may indicate that he enjoyed a position of relative privilege or high status.
The early date for the burial is interesting, placing it in a period in Ireland that saw the arrival of Bishop Pallidius in 431 and the unfolding of St Patrick‘s mission, both ministering to fledgling Christian communities; a time when newly adopted Christian modes of burial were competing with older Pagan practises. This form of burial - slab-lined with extended inhumation, aligned E-W, head to the W, devoid of grave goods - is first practised during this period, and is often interpreted as indicative of a Christian burial. The date of the burial also suggests that this man lived in a settlement that pre-dated the construction of the two raths, which crown elevated ground to E and W of the grave. (Seaver 2022)

source_data.original_text:
In January 2011 ancient human skeletal remains were found lying on a rocky shoreline, c. 60m S of Cahermore cliff-edge fort (SL016-001001-). The discovery was reported to the Gardaí, and subsequently to the National Museum of Ireland, who carried out an excavation on 17th January 2011 to record and retrieve the remains (Halpin 2011). The burial was located on or within a sloping ramp-like deposit of silty, stony soil, which was partly covered with storm beach deposit, large limestone blocks, and broken slabs of concrete, which had been dumped on the shore in recent years. 
The extended skeleton was oriented on a NE-SW axis, with the head to the SW. The skull was missing, except for a fragment of mandible (jaw), and the left arm and most of the legs were also missing. No trace of a grave cut or structure was found: The excavator received the impression that the body was placed on a stony, silty deposit and then covered with further stones (Halpin 2011).
Osteological analysis of the bones determined that the skeleton was that of a man, 35-45 years at the time of death, approximately 170cm (5 feet 7 inches) in height during life. He had endured poor dental health, including calculus build-up and periodontitis. Evidence of dental enamel hypoplasia indicated that he might have suffered an illness or period of malnutrition during childhood. He also had low-grade osteoarthritis in the left hip and an os acromiale lesion in the left shoulder blade, both conditions suggesting wear and tear of the bones due to a relatively active lifestyle. Periosteal reactions noted in the left ankle may reflect an injury or possibly an instance of infectious disease, which was still active at the time of the man’s death (Keating 2011).

Situated on the riverward crest of one of the grass-covered terraces that constitute the E-side of the Easky valley. This enclosure is subrectangular (28m NW-SE; 23m NNE-SSW) in plan, and is enclosed by a drystone wall (Wth c.3m; int. H 1.25m; ext. H 1.5m) with the lower courses of boulders. The enclosing wall is truncated at WNW by a later field boundary, on a NNE–SSW axis. The interior slopes down from E to W. A line of boulders, with a bank (H 0.6m) or accumulation of soil on its E side, extends from the enclosing wall at N for several meters through the interior to S. It lies c. 3.5m E of the W side of the enclosure. Conjoined to the E side of the enclosure, is a second, smaller, subrectangular enclosure (SL017-022002-). The shared wall between the two enclosures is most substantial at its N and S end but is narrower in between. There is no gap evident allowing access from one enclosure to the other. 

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

source_data.original_text:
Situated on the riverward crest of one of the grass-covered terraces that constitute the E-side of the Easky valley. This enclosure is subrectangular or roughly D-shaped (17.5m NE-SW; 15m NW-SE) in plan and is enclosed by a stone bank (int. H 0.4; ext. H 0.7-1m). It is conjoined on its W side to a larger subrectangular enclosure (SL017-022001-). The shared wall between the two enclosures is most substantial at its N and S end but is narrower in between. There is no gap evident allowing access from one enclosure to the other. In the interior of this enclosure, an internal dividing wall extends in an arc from the enclosure wall at W to meet the enclosure wall at S, defining a subtriangular space (9.4m NW-SE; 6.5m NE-SW) in the SW quadrant. A gap, flanked by two orthostats, in the internal wall allows access to the space. The enclosed space encompasses a raised area or platform. On top of the platform is a semicircular setting of split boulders, possibly a hut site (SL017-022003-). In the NW quadrant of the enclosure is a second raised platform. Immediately to the E of this are the foundations of a rectangular stone-built house (SL017-022004-). Adjacent to the enclosure wall in the SE quadrant is a third small, irregular-shaped building (SL017-022005-).

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

In an enclosure (SL017-022002-). This consists of a semi-circular (diam. c. 4.5-5m) setting of large split stones, possibly the basal course of a hut site. It is built on a raised area or platform enclosed within a subtriangular space (9.4m NW-SE; 6.5m NE-SW) in the SW quadrant of the enclosure.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

In an enclosure (SL017-022002-). In the SE quadrant of the enclosure is an irregularly-shaped structure (L 4.6m E-W) defined by a basal course comprising firmly-set stone blocks. It has  remnants of a possible internal division and was interpreted by the fieldworker as an outbuilding rather than a habitation site.

source_data.original_text:
Locating in old turf cuttings, on a broad, flat expanse of bog bordered at E by the valley of the Buncrowey River and at W by a small stream valley. There is a forestry plantation c. 40 m to SE. This monument was exposed during turf cutting in the 1960s. When first inspected in 1963, it was partly concealed by peat layers and consisted of a central cairn or pile of stones, incorporating hearths or areas of burning. The cairn was enclosed by a narrow fosse. Small timber stakes were lying in a horizontal position in the bottom of the fosse. Immediately outside the fosse was a low enclosing wall (Wth c. 1m; H 0.45m) of small rounded boulders.  Further turf cutting during the 1960’s exposed more of the cairn (SMR file).  When inspection in 1994, the monument was visible as a cairn (5.5m NW–SE; 4m NE–SW; H c. 0.7m) located off-centre within an irregular enclosing wall, partly concealed by bushes and bog regeneration. The poorly preserved wall enclosed an area c. 11m NW–SE by 9.5m NE–SW. The fosse between the cairn and the enclosing wall was no longer evident.  An inspection in 2014 found that the cairn is evident only as a slight rise (c. 6-7m N–S; c. 5m E–W; H c. 0.3-0.4m) entirely engulfed in thick heather, with small willow scrub at the N end.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 18 August 2014

Within a forestry plantation, situated on the broad, flat, bog-covered crest of the E side of the Easky River valley. This monument was exposed and largely cleared of peat c. 1970. Subcircular cist (1.25m N-S; 0.9m E-W) defined by ten principal upright stones (H 0.4-0.75) set into the pre-bog soil, with a further stone set externally in the SE corner. All have their long axes aligned with the perimeter. Two stones inside the cist at NE do not sit well with the overall pattern of the wall but seem sufficently tightly set to be structural. The arrangement of the structural stones has a well defined E-W axis, most strikingly illustrated by the arrangment of three larger and higher stones at both the NW and SE corners.

Locating in an area of cutaway blanket bog, with scattered, active areas of small-scale machine turf harvesting, on a broad, flat-topped N–S ridge. The E side of the ridge falls into the Easkey River valley. This record was not listed in the SMR (1989). It was listed in the RMP (1995) as ‘field system -pre-bog’ but no source of information or field description was added to the file at that time. The area was inspection in 2014. Remnants of three possible field walls were found. At ITM 538582 827171 a cropmark of low heather highlights a linear concentration (Wth 0.7-1m) of stones which can be traced in a shallow arc NNW–SSE for 19-20m. The stones protrude only slightly above the bog surface but appear densely packed. Located 35m to SE at ITM 538616 827120 is a short length of possible wall (Wth 0.7m) which is visible as a concentration of stones (Wth 0.7m) extending for 4-5m on a NW–SE axis. It is bisected on a WNW–ESE axis a by a linear peat bank (Wth 1m; H 0.4m). Located 10m to ESE at ITM 538618 827111 is another short length of possible wall consisting of a concentration (Wth 0.8-1m) of stones barely protruding from the bog surface. It can be traced for 3m on a NE–SW axis. The relationship between the three discrete lengths of wall is unknown, and it is not possible to reconstruct the original pattern of the field system.

source_data.original_text:
In a thicket of gorse bushes, located in a broad, flat expanse of heather and rush-covered bog in the valley of the Easkey River. The river is c. 400m to E. There is a portal tomb (SL017-021----) c. 80m to ESE. A low, roughly oval concentration or cairn (c. 12m E–W; c. 7m N–S) of moss and sod-covered stones, partly submerged in flat, boggy ground. The surface is uneven, rising and falling in irregular-shaped humps and hollows. Several large stones protrude from the surface, especially along the N perimeter, many entangled in the twisting roots of gorse bushes. At the E end of the cairn, there is a roughly square, vertical-sided pit (1.4m N–S; c. 1.4m E–W; D 0.4m) sunk into the peat. The W side of the pit is faced with a single upright slab (L at least 1.2m N–S). Its height above the wet peat which forms the floor of the cavity is 0.4m but it is set to a depth of at least 0.2m into the peat. The N side of the cavity is faced with drystone walling (H 0.4m above peat) consisting of five courses of thin, horizontally laid slabs. On the S side of the cavity are a number of close-set, medium-sized stones. Covering the cavity is a large capstone (L c. 1.2m N–S; c. 1.3m E–W; T 0.2m). The top of the slab is flush with surface ground level. It rests on the N and S side walls but there is a gap between it and the W side wall. The under-surface of the slab can be seen to slope sharply downwards so that its E end is level with the floor of the pit, thus obscuring that side of the pit. Located 5m to W of the stone-lined pit, a boulder (1.5m N–S; 1m E–W; H 0.4m) protrudes from a hollow in the cairn surface. It rests on a number of smaller stones and overlies a small cavity. A further 1.5m to W of this, there is a stone bank or ‘wall’ (Wth 2-2.4m; H 0.4-0.6m) of loose, jumbled stones, which defines the W end of the cairn, describing a shallow arc S-W–N. A few isolated upright stones protrude from the bog c. 2m to W of the cairn.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 17 April 2014

In pasture, located at the N edge of on a broad, low hill or elevation of dry, grass-covered ground, surrounded at NW–S by lowlying, heather and rush-grown boggy ground. A subcircular, or roughly square, grass-covered mound or platform (c. 5m NNW–SSE; 4m ENE–WSW; H 0.7-0.8m) defined around its perimeter at W, N and E by a scarp with a slightly raised rim on top, and incorporated on the S side into a relict earth and stone field boundary (SL017-097002-) which extends beyond the structure to WSW. Large stones protrude from the sod around the perimeter. On the W side and E sides the scarp appears somewhat irregular or indented. On the E side there is a roughly C-shaped indentation (1.4m NW–SE; c. 1m NE–SW) partly lined with stones. A single upright stone (H 0.5m), almost triangular in shape, protrudes from the relatively flat top of the platform at SW. The function and date of this structure is unclear. It may be the remains of some form of vernacular kiln, but it could be a cairn or even a hut site. There is another structure (SL017-098001-), an enclosure (SL017-098002-), a possible enclosure (SL017-098003-) and an unclassified cairn (SL017-099----) c. 100m to SE, towards the S side of the same hill.

In pasture, on the level top of a broad, low hill which forms a virtual island of elevated ground surrounded at W–S by lowlying wet, boggy ground. Located within a rectangular field, abutting the drystone field wall which borders the SW side of the field. This consists of a roughly D-shaped sunken area (8m NW–SE; 3.6m NE–SW), with a flat-based interior which is 0.45m lower than the level of the surrounding field. It is bordered on the straight SW side by a NW–SE drystone field wall (Wth 0.8; H 1.4m), and elsewhere by an inward-facing scarp, lined with a ruined wall (Wth c. 0.8m; int. H 0.55-0.6m; ext. H 0.2m) of moss-covered stones. Within the sunken interior, there is a small, subcircular stone feature, located midway along the NW/SE field wall. It consists of a low platform (diam. 2m; H 0.3-0.4m) of medium to large-sized stones, one stone high, flanked on its SW side by a short section of drystone wall (Wth 0.8m; H 1.4m) which projects 0.2-0.3m to NE out from the NW–SE field wall. The D-shaped structure is surrounded on the NW, NE and SE sides by the remains of a roughly rectangular enclosure (SL017-098002-). In the SE corner of the same field, there is a cairn (SL017-099----). Abutting the opposite, W face, of the extant NW–SE field wall on the SW side of the sunken structure, is a D-shaped platform or possible enclosure (SL017-098002-). Located c. 100m to NE there is a structure (SL017-097001-) incorporated into a field boundary (SL017-097002-). These remains are not shown on the 1837 or 1913 OS 6-inch maps. They are difficult to interpret: their function and date are unclear. It seems likely that they are post-medieval in date; they may relate to a vernacular settlement.

Located c. 100m to NE there is a structure (SL017-097001-) incorporated into a field boundary (SL017-097002-). These remains are not shown on the 1837 or 1913 OS 6-inch maps. Situated on the SW edge of a low rise in poorly drained pasture. Raised circular area (23.3m E-W; 22.5m N-S) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 4-5m; int. H 0.3-0.6m; ext. H 1.8-2m), faced internally with stone at the W. At the outer foot of the bank is a fosse (Wth 2-2.5m) with an external bank (Wth 4-5.5m; int. H 1.6m; ext. H 1.3m). The inner bank is very low on its internal face and has been levelled at NE. The fosse is well defined except at E where it is evident only as a shallow depression. T he outer bank is best preserved on the W half of the rath but is low at E and has been truncated by an E–W field fence at S. The interior slopes down gently from SW to E. A sod-covered line of stones, on a NW–SE axis, traverses the interior to NE of centre. A gap (Wth 3m) in outer bank at E may mark the original entrance.

source_data.original_text:
Located in rough-average pasture, tending to be wet and poorly drained. Situated c. 45m NW of Farranmacfarrell House, a possible 17th-century house (SL018-096----). A wooded area is indicated at this location on the 1837 OS 6-inch map. A subcircular hachured enclosure is shown on the 1913 edition. Circular area (diam. 30m) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 2.8-3.4m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.6m ,at W), largely levelled at NE–S, and enclosed at S–NW by a fosse (Wth 3m; ext. D 1m). Outside the fosse at NW there is a remnant of an earthen bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 1.4m; ext. H 0.9m), with external stone facing. On the 1913 OS 6-inch map this is shown as part of a field boundary which curved around the enclosure at NW–N. An inspection in 2001 determined that this enclosure is probably a tree-ring or designed  landscape feature.  

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date revised upload: 20 July 2015

Situated on a N-facing slope in hilly pasture. Cashelboy church (SL018-029002-) is 5.5m E. Late 16th century, square, two-storey, limestone-built tower house (dim. 7.7m - Wall T 1.4m) with a slight base batter. There is a N-S barrel vault over ground floor level with loft over. The entrance, at the S end of the E wall, gives access to the vaulted area. A spiral stairwell immediately N of the entrance gives access to first floor level. The stairwell is lit by a single slit ope at ground floor level and by two others at first floor level. At first floor level an intermural passage in the S wall leads to a garderobe in the SW angle. An intermural passage commencing in the NE angle leads to an oubliette in the centre of the E wall. There are a number of windows at first floor level. In the E wall is a large round-headed window with late 16th century dressing and in the N wall a small slit ope. There are broken-out, flat-headed, single-light windows in the W and S walls. There are large rectangular niches on either side of the windows in the W and N walls. There is no evidence for a second floor or for battlements.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
On a terrace of gently undulating pasture, broken in parts by rock outcropping, bordered at E by a river ravine. This field system consist of a regular grid of rectangular fields covering an area of c. 400m N-S by c. 250m E-W. At the E and SE there is a concentration of smaller fields (c. 55-60m NE-SW and 25-35m NW-SE) defined by low sod-covered banks/walls (Wth c. 1.8-2.3m; H 0.5-0.8m), covering an area of c. 200m N-S by 125m E-W. Abutting one of the field boundaries are the wall-footings of a rectangular two-roomed house (SL018-045002-) suggesting that some of the smaller fields represent garden plots associated with a small settlement. Towards the SE there is an area of relatively recent small scale quarrying (SL018-045001-). At its S end, the field system incorporates the enclosing elements of a ringfort/cashel (SL018-046001-). To W and N the faint outlines are visible of levelled field boundaries enclosing larger rectangular fields (c. 65-75 NE-SW; c. 80-150m NW-SE) with traces of cultivation ridges. The field system and the rectangular house appear to post-date the ringfort and may be post-1700 in date.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 27 January 2014

source_data.original_text:
This record refers to the remains of a bank or wall enclosing a roughly D-shaped area, which may originally have been circular (diam. c. 85-90m). The wall/bank roughly follows the lower contours of a natural elevation. At SW–N it can be traced as a low, degraded stony rise (Wth c. 2m). At N–SE, it is reduced to a scarp (ext. H 1m at SE), and at S it is truncated by a modern road (N59). Centrally located within the enclosure, on the summit of the elevation, is a cashel (SL018-046001-). The intervening gap between the cashel and the enclosure bank/wall measures c. 20-25m and is sub-divided by transverse walls. The date of the enclosure is uncertain. It is possible that the enclosure is contemporary with the cashel and represents an outer enclosing bank of the cashel. Alternatively the enclosure may relate to the incorporation of the cashel into a later field system (SL018-045003-). It is recorded in an aerial photograph (ACP V203/ 134-3; roll 128, print 1).

In pasture, extending across a series of natural terraces on the W-facing slope of Red Hill. The remains of a series of rectangular and subrectangular fields defined by low and largely levelled earth and stones bank (Wth. 0.8-1.2m; H 0.3m). The field boundaries extend on NNW–SSE and WNW–ESE axes but the remains are fragmentary and it is not possible to trace the full outline of the fields. Recorded in an aerial photograph (ACAP V203/133-3, Roll 127 Pr. 33). Butting one of the field boundaries is a possible enclosure (SL018-050002-), and towards E end of the field system, is another enclosure (SL019-259----). Located c. 200-250m to S of these enclosures, there are a megalithic structure (SL018-051001-), a cashel (SL018-051002-), an enclosure (SL018-051002-) and another field system (SL018-051009-).

In rough to average pasture, in an area of sharply undulating terrain overlooked to E by Red Hill. Located towards the SW end of a NE–SW ridge, with a steep fall of ground at SE and also at W–SW. At E there is a gentler slope. Slightly raised oval area (29m N–S; 18.5m E–W) defined by degraded remnants of a stone wall (ext. H 0.5m at E, 1.4m at W). The interior ground surface is uneven and strewn with sod-covered stones. At the inner face of the cashel wall in the SW quadrant there is an opening into a souterrain (SL018-051003-). Immediately to N of the opening, there is a linear surface depression, extending from the cashel wall into the interior to ENE for c. 7m, which appears to indicate the line of the souterrain. The cashel is dilapidated and poorly preserved. There is an enclosure (SL018-051004-) immediately to E.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
In a cashel (SL018-051002-). Marked as 'Cave' on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. An opening in the inner face of the ruined enclosing wall of the cashel at SW gives access to a souterrain with walls of drystone construction and lintel roofing. A sketch plan recorded in 1986 (SMR Files) shows that the access hole leads into a chamber which is connected at its E end by a low lintelled creepway to a second chamber. The second chamber has a small stone lined cupboard built into its E wall. Opening from the N wall of the second chamber is another creepway which is blocked but appears to extends to N. At ground level in the cashel interior, just to N of the souterrain access hole, a linear surface depression is evident extending from the cashel wall into the interior to ENE for c. 7m. This appears to indicated the line of the souterrain. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 15 July 2013

In rough to average pasture, in an area of sharply undulating terrain overlooked to E by Red Hill. Located towards the SW end of a NE–SW ridge, with a steep fall of ground at SE and also at W–SW. This broadly oval or subcircular enclosure (19m N–S; c. 15m E–W) has been partly levelled. It is defined N–SSE by a low sod-covered stony bank (Wth 1.5m; int. H 0.25m; ext. H 0.6m, at E), and at S–NNW by a slight undulation. It is bisected, to W of centre, by a later field fence on a NNW–SSE axis, which appears as a sod-covered stone bank (Wth 1.2m; H 0.3-0.5m), with a field ditch (Wth 1.6m; D 0.3m) on its W side. There is a cashel (SL018-051002-) immediately to W of the enclosure.

In rough to average pasture, in an area of sharply undulating terrain, located on a ridge top bordered at S-W by a fall of ground into a stream valley, and overlooked to E by the rising slopes of Red Hill. Listed as ‘earthworks’in the RMP (1995) on the basis of features visible in an aerial photograph (ACP V 203/133-2; Roll 127, print 32). The features visible in the aerial photograph cover an area of c. 130m N-S by c. 140m E-W and consist of ruined field boundaries, seams of natural rock-outcropping, and areas of quarrying. The field boundaries represent the fragmentary remains of a field system. At ground level, the field boundaries are apparent only as low, sod-covered linear rises (Wth 1-2m; H 0.3-0.75m) from which stones protrude intermittently. The remains are fragmentary, and it is not possible to trace a coherent pattern of ancient fields. The field boundaries skirt or abut a number of other monuments, including a megalithic structure (SL018-051001-), a cashel (SL018-051002-), an enclosure (SL018-051004-), and two possible hut sites (SL018-051006-; SL018-051008-).

In pasture, located on a ridge top, in an area of sharply undulating terrain, broken by rock outcropping and traversed by remnants of field boundaries (SL018-051009-). There is a megalithic structure (SL018-051001-) 6m to N. This consists of a roughly C-shaped structure (8m NE–SW; c. 6m NW–SE) defined at NE–SW by a broadly slumped, sod-covered stone and earth bank (Wth 1.8-2m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.2-0.3m at E). Cutting across the open side at NW is a sod-covered NE–SW field bank. A gap (Wth 1m) in the field bank allows access into the enclosed C-shaped area. It was recorded as a possible fulacht fia in 1986 in a sketch plan (SMR file: pers. comm. W. Forbes, mound ‘A’). It is not a fulacht fia. It may have been a small animal pen or enclosure, or a hut site.

In rough pasture, situated at the edge of a high bluff at the S side of an E-facing slope overlooking a bend in the River Dunneill. Depicted as a circular enclosure on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map. Substantially raised, subcircular platform (14.7m N-S; 12m E-W, at top) with steeply sloping, almost vertical, sides (H 1.3m at W, 3m at E). At S the platform merges with the cliff face of the bluff. The flat top of the platform is defined on its perimeter at W by remnants of a bank (Wth c. 0.8m). On the S edge of the platform are the remnants of modern stone wall, on a roughly E–W axis, which forms a barrier along the cliff edge. A farm track skirts the enclosure at N.

Situated on the N-facing slope of a low rise in rough boggy pasture. Not marked on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map. An intermittent row of low stones extends, on a NE–SW axis, between the SE side of an enclosure (SL018-058002-) and the SW side of a possible stone circle (SL018-059001-), a distance of c. 35m. The line of stones appears to continue for c. 5m to NE of the stone circle. The stones appear to be set on edge but are very low, and are concealed by, or barely protruding above, the bog vegetation. At the SW end of their extent, close to the enclosure (SL018-058002-), the stones are 1-2m apart but the spacing increases to c. 10m as they approach the stone circle (SL018-059001-). Situated on top of a S-facing slope overlooking a ford in a small WNW-ESE river a short distance below. Raised circular platform (diam. c. 30m) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 5.4m; int. H 0.85m; ext. c. 3m) with evidence for both internal and external stone revetment. The bank has been incorporated into a field boundary at NNW-SSE. At the foot of the mound from WSW-NW is a wide, deep fosse (Wth 3m; ext. D 1.2m) with a flat-topped rise (Wth. 4.2m; H 1.1m) at its outer lip which may be the remains of an original outer bank. At the foot of the mound at S the fosse changes form to a terrace (Wth 5m) on the steep slope overlooking the stream. The SE quadrant of the interior has been quarried out. A modern farm road skirts the rath at NE-SE. 

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

Located in a broad expanse of sedge- and heather-covered bog, bordered to W by the valley of the Croagh River. The bog is cut through in parts by old turf cuttings, drainage ditches and bog roads. A bog road is located c. 20m to SW of the hut site. H 0.4m) protrude at SW–NW. The stones appear to be part of an enclosing wall, almost entirely engulfed in peat and overgrowth. The interior is is marked by bog grasses, mosses and a dense growth of rushes.

The first three are located along the SE side of a NE-SW drain. There are intervening spaces of 30m and 35m between them. The fourth lies at the NW side of the drain. The drain cuts through the SW side where the trough was presumably located.

In the base of the Crowagh River valley, on a broad U-shaped area of level, grassy ground defined by a meander in the river.  Immediately to W of the river, the valley slope rises steeply to a plateau of blanket bog which stretching to the W. The well consists of a rectangular, vertical-sided pit (2.4m NE–SW; 1.1m NW–SE; D 0.5m) with a narrow outflow channel extending from the N corner for 4m to the river bank at NNW. Several large stones form a rough surround or paving at the S–SW end of the well. According to local information, the well is known as ‘The Blessed Well’ but it is not associated with a saint, and there is no tradition of a pattern or a ‘cure’. The well was used by turf harvesters as a source of fresh water.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 4 April 2014

Located in the SW corner of a roughly rectangular turf cutting, on a flat plateau of heather and sedge-covered blanket bog bordered at NE–E by the Crowagh River valley. A roughly circular area (diam. c. 5.5-6m) can be distinguished by a slightly denser, higher growth of heather. Exposed on its perimeter at SE–SW is a shallow arc of low close-set stones, possibly the remnants of a stone bank or wall. The stone bank/wall (Wth 0.4-0.7m) appears to be only two stones wide, and barely protrudes above the bog surface. Individual stones can be glimpsed or felt by probing beneath the heather elsewhere around the perimeter of the heather cropmark. The visible remains suggest that a circular stone structure, possibly a hut site, is concealed beneath the heather.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 2 July 2014

source_data.original_text:
Located on gently elevated ground in the SW quadrant of the enclosure (SL018-095001-), on a strip of land flanked at W by the Ballyglass River and at E by the Doonbeakin River. The souterrain is of drystone construction with lintel roofing. A rectangular surface depression encloses an access hole (1.6m NE–SW; 0.65m NW–SE) through the roof of the souterrain, created by the displacement of a stone roof lintel.  It opens onto the SE end of a roughly oval chamber (3.62m NW–SE; 1.8m NE–SW; H c. 1.36m). The floor of the chamber slopes down gently towards the NW, and is covered in loose stone rubble. At the N corner of the NW end of the chamber, the two side walls converge at an opening (Wth 0.6m NE–SW; H c. 0.96m) to a short blind passage (L 1.66m NW–SE) which curves slightly to NW. There is no obvious evidence for a continuation of the souterrain to NW or N from this passage. At the SE end of the oval chamber, the two side walls converge at an opening into a cupboard-like recess or small chamber (L 1.07m NE–SW; Wth 0.75m NW–SE at entrance, expanding to 1.18m at back wall; H 0.76m) which is trapezoidal in plan. It has space sufficient only for one person to crouch in. A large flat slab serves as a threshold stone at the entrance, and is set higher than the floor of the oval chamber. The floor of the little chamber is paved with slabs. The roof is formed by stone lintels. These are arranged so that there is one central, recessed square lintel (0.59m NW–SE; 0.46-0.59m NE–SW). This may be an original trapdoor entrance to the souterrain, dropping from ground surface into the small trapezoidal chamber which served as an antechamber to the large oval chamber. Beneath the threshold stone of the antechamber is a partly concealed opening into a creep or low, narrow passage (Wth c. 0.75m). The passage slopes down beneath the small chamber/antechamber, the threshold stone of which serves as the first roof lintel of the passage. It is filled with stone rubble but can be seen to continue for at least 2m to SE. There is a field clearance cairn (3m N–S; 3.5m E–W; H 0.8m) immediately to E of the access hole to the souterrain, and a second field clearance cairn (diam. 4m; H 1.1m) is located 3m to E of that. A bank/scarp, with a pronounced external face (H 0.85m) and a slight internal lip (Wth c. 2m), skirts the two cairns and the souterrain at S–W, defining the elevated ground on which they are located. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 8 July 2014

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a strip (Wth 100-200m) of gently elevated, level ground bordered by the Ballyglass River at W and the Doonbeakin River at E. A ford on the Ballyglass River is shown on 1913 OS 6-inch map c. 45m to NW of the enclosure, adjacent to a ruined vernacular farmstead. The two rivers converge c. 200m to N of the enclosure where other fording points are shown on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. Ovoid area (82m N–S; 67m E–W) defined by a sod-covered, ruined drystone wall. The W half of the enclosure encompasses higher, level ground from where there is a gentle slope to N and NE where the ground levels out again. At W and N the wall is incorporated into field plots associated with the adjacent vernacular cottage. The interior of the enclosure is bisected centrally, on an E–W axis, by a ruined, largely sod-covered drystone wall (Wth 1m; H 0.6m), roughly built of rounded boulders. There is a souterrain (SL018-095----) in the elevated SW quadrant of the interior. Immediately to E of the access hole to the souterrain, there is a grass-covered, circular field clearance cairn (3m N–S; 3.5m E–W; H 0.8m). A second cairn (diam. 4m; H 1.1m) is located 3m to E of that. A bank/scarp (H 0.85m) skirts the two cairns and the souterrain at S–W, defining the elevated ground on which they are located. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 8 July 2014

source_data.original_text:
Situated in relatively level pasture. Stone-built house with high gables, two storeys with attic. An extension, probably later in date, extends the full length of the SSE wall. In the centre of the NNW wall at ground floor level is a semi-circular headed doorway flanked on either side by two large rectangular windows. There are five similar rectangular windows in the same wall at first floor level. There are two small rectangular windows at attic level in both the ENE and WSW gables. A chimney stack in the ENE gable may be a later addition. There are a number of small, squat windows in the extension. A relatively modern, although now disused, building has been appended to the SSE of the house.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Located on the S bank of a meandering stream, in a small valley, bordered to S by an expanse of blanket bog. It is situated in the NW corner of a pasture field which was reclaimed from the bog. There is a court tomb (SL018-076----) c. 40m to NE. The burnt mound is exposed in section at the junction of the E–W stream gully and a N–S field drain/property fence. It is visible as a layer (L c. 4m E-W; D 0.2m) of black, charcoal-rich soil incorporating small angular stones and charcoal fragments in the S side of the stream gully at a height of c. 1.5m above the stream. At the W end, the layer can be traced extending c. 3-4m to S in the side of a U-shaped cutting through the stream scarp, at the N end of the N–S field drain. A layer of peat (D 0.2-0.3m) overlies the burnt material. The outline of the mound can not be traced at ground surface.

Situated immediately W of a holy well (SL019-006001-), on the N verge of a modern roadway. This monument consists of a tall, square pillar (H c. 3m; Wth. 0.85m) constructed of cut limestone, and topped with a triangular stone-built cap. It stands on a stepped stone plinth. At the upper portion of the S face of the pillar there is a Latin inscription carved in relief which translates as 'Eugene McDonnell, Vicar of this district, had me erected 1591'. (Ordnance Survey 1836, 315 (130); Kilgannon 1926, 295). There is a church (SL019-007001-) and graveyard (SL019-007002-) 80m to WSW.

The church was built on a site previously granted to Saint Columba (ibid). The Visitation Book of 1615 mentions that' the church and chancel were thatched' (ibid).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture/grazing, located on the N-facing slopes and terraces of a large limestone hill which is named Red Hill on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. A system of relict field walls can be traced over an extensive area on the hill, overlain by the regular grid of extant walls which define the current property divisions. Some of the relict walls are depicted on the 1837 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps. In some areas the walls are visible as low, sod-covered stone banks (Wth 1.2-2m; H 0.2-0.5m), and in other areas, they are reduced to gapped lines of individual stones. For the most part, the walls respect the natural contours and terracing on the hill, and appear to have enclosed subrectangular and irregular-shaped fields on the level terraces. The remains are, however, fragmentary and a complete pattern of fields cannot be traced, nor is it possible to determine to what extent the various isolated wall fragments are contemporary with each other. Within the field system are a court tomb (SL019-011----), several enclosures (SL019-003----; SL019-008002-; SL019-008004-; SL019-008006-; SL019-009----; SL019-010----), hut sites (SL019-008001-; SL019-008007-; SL019-008008-), and a church (SL019-007001-) and graveyard (SL019-007002-).

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 1 September 2014

source_data.original_text:
Located in level, gently elevated pasture, adjacent to the E boundary of the townland. It is overlooked 400m to W by Skreen Hill; immediately to N, ground falls away gradually to NE, providing excellent views over a broad sweep of coastal grassland, with Ben Bulben and Knocknarae visible on the far horizon. A stream, which marks the S boundary of the townland, is located 300m to S.
This rath is not indicated on the 1837 OS 6-inch map; on the 1913 edition, it is shown in hachured outline as an oval enclosure (32m ENE−WSW; 21m NNW−SSE) defined by a bank, truncated on its SW side, and partly on the NE and SE edges, by later linear field boundaries which tightly box in the rath on four sides.
These field boundaries are extant, and the rectangular space they enclosure is largely covered by a dense thicket of blackthorn, elder and brambles, with the densest scrub in the area of the rath. 
The outline of the rath cannot now be traced; the enclosing bank appears to have been largely or entirely levelled, although it is possible that remnants may survive at E or SE, where the overgrowth is impenetrable and inspection was impossible. The interior of the rath does not appear to have been raised significantly above surrounding ground level. A low, subcircular grassy rise (diam. 6-8m; H 0.3-0.4m) towards the W end of the rath interior marks the location of a souterrain (SL019-018002-).

source_data.original_text:
Located in a rath (SL019-018001-).
This souterrain is not shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map; on the 1913 edition it is indicated as ‘Cave’. A low, grass-grown subcircular rise (diam. 6-8m; H 0.3-0.4m) at the W end of the rath interior marks the location. There are two surface openings 6m apart, one at the NE and one at the SW end of the rise. There reveal the souterrain to be of drystone construction. The NE opening (c. 0.6m NE−SW; c. 0.5m NW−SE; D c. 0.5m) reveals an in situ lintel above a passage, largely infilled with earth, which appears to extend to SW. In the opening (c. 0.8m NW−SE; c. 0.8m NE−SW) at the SW end of the rise, drystone walling and a probably in situ lintel can be glimpsed, and a partly infilled or collapsed passage appears to extend to N or NW.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on level, gently elevated ground, bordered 8m to E by a stream which flows N-NE through an expanse of flat, damp ground, marked by a dense growth of rushes and yellow flag. Raised circular platform (30.5m E–W; 29m N–S) defined by a scarp (Wth slope 2-3m; ext. H 1.4-1.6m). Stones protrude randomly in parts from the sod covering of the scarp. Outside the scarp at NNE–E there is a very shallow depression (Wth 3m), with a hint of slightly raised lip or bank (Wth c. 2m) on its outer edge. The original entrance is not clear: there is a low area or slump (Wth c. 2m) in the enclosing scarp at SW but this is not clearly defined, and another slump or possible break in the scarp is located at SE but this is largely obscured by brambles and hawthorn bushes. The rath interior appears generally flat and level, but in the E half there is a very slight incline down to E and SE, and a broad, shallow depression (Wth c. 6m) is evident in the SW quadrant.

Within a relatively large, modern field. Not marked on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. Identified from aerial photography. In the SW is a small D-shaped area (dims. 13m E-W; 10.6m N-S) bordered on the straight W side by a linear field wall and from N-E-S by a curving, sod-covered stony bank (Wth. 3m - 3.5m; int H 0.8m; ext H 0.2m - 0.6m. At the E end of the rise is a roughly circular (diam c.5m), sod-covered heap of field stones. To the W of this scarp is an area of wet ground bordered by a slight scarp. raw_items.raw_text: before they community settled at Boyle, Co. Roscommon (1970, 363)

raw_items.basis: Boyle Abbey context; Cistercian grange period

source_data.original_text:
Gwynn and Hadcock regard as doubtful the possible establishment of a Cistercian foundation at ‘Ballinley or Ballinig’ which had been suggested, was occupied before they community settled at Boyle, Co. Roscommon (1970, 363). The site is known locally as the 'Abbey Field' and a stoup (SL019-043002-) is incorporated into a field wall to the SE. In addition, there is a possible font or benniter (SL019-193----) used as a garden ornament at Ballinlig House, c. 200m to the NW. Given the local placename tradition coupled with the presence of the stoup and possible benniter it is possible that this reflects some element of a religious presence. The possibility that this may be site of a grange belonging to Boyle abbey cannot be ruled out.

The remains are indicated as field boundaries on the OS 6-inch maps though the site is not named. It is situated on a natural ridge projection and the SW of the site utilises the precipitous slope of the ridge.  It consists of a raised rectangular area (82m NW-SE; 62.5m NE-SW) defined by a scarp (H 1.6-2.3m). At the NE side and at the NE end of the NW side are traces of a possible levelled bank at the upper edge of the scarp. At the SE side the perimeter has either been destroyed or incorporated into modern field boundary walls. At the ENE angle an irregularly-shaped piles of loose stone may mark the site of a tower or other building. At the foot of the scarp at the NE and NW sides is a wide, deep fosse (Wth 7.7m; D 1.6m). At the NW end of the SW side this is disturbed by a modern drain. At the NW end of the SW side the fosse is absent and there is a terrace from which the ground drops steeply for several metres. At the outer lip of the fosse at the NE end of the SE side is a low outer bank (Wth 6m; H 0.45m). The outline of this bank may also be traced at the NW side where it has been incorporated into a modern wall. A depression (Wth c. 15m) in the scarp close to centre of NW side, with accompanying causeway and blocked up break in outer bank, marks the original entrance. Outside of this a relatively steep slope falls to the estuary of the River Finn a short distance below. Immediately SE of centre in the interior, are the remains of a rectangular building (17.2m WNW-ESE; 7.5m NNE-SSW) defined by a low, grass-covered bank (Wth c. 1.6m; H 0.35m) of earth and stone. The function of this structure is unknown but it may be the remains of a barn or granary.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan, Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 9 April 2014

This monument straddles the narrow spine of a low N-S ridge overlooking the W side of Ballisodare Bay. Approximately oval-shaped platform (dims. 47.3m N-S; 30m E-W) atop a steep-sided mound (H 2m). At the upper edge of the scarp at N and E are traces of levelled bank. At the foot of the mound is a space (Wth. 7m - 7.4m) beyond which from SE-S-SW and from N-NNE-NE is a substantial bank of earth and stone (Wth. 7m; H 0.7m). At E and W this merges with the naturally-occurring slope of the ridge. At N it survives as a scarp (H 0.7m). Original entrance may have been at SW (Wth.3m). Within the N half of the internal area is a possible hut site (SL019-056003-). At N is a break in the outer bank (Wth. 5m - 6m). The terminals merge with the series of disused field banks which encompass the top of the ridge upon which the rath is sited (see SL019-056002-).

One of seven middens (SL019-057001-, SL019-057002-, SL019-057003-, SL019-057004-, SL019-057005-, SL019-057006-, SL019-057007-) identified along a 1.3km length of shoreline on the W side of Ballisodare Bay, four in Tanrego West townland and three in Tanrego East or Carrowmore townland. This large midden follows the curve of the coastline for c.40m. On inspection in 1994 it was found to be composed of a layer of oyster shells with smaller quantities of periwinkle and limpet shells (D 1m - 1.2m). A hearth was also identified. The midden is directly beneath the sod and is underlain by a compact orange, sandy subsoil. In places, where the underlying layer has been undercut by wave action, the midden layer forms an overhang. A late-17th century copper alloy token was recovered from this midden in 2000: it is in the National Museum of Ireland  (pers. comm. M.A. Timoney). (Synge 1985, 128)

source_data.original_text:
Situated in level pasture close to the W shore of Ballisodare Bay. O'Rorke (1890, 392) referred to 'an old castle and bawn, in fair preservation…in Tanrego. There are no upstanding remains of the castle (SL019-062001-). The bawn, of late 17th or 18th century date, comprising a quadrangular area (c .30-34m N-S; c. 24m E-W) defined by substantial walls of mortared limestone (Wall T 1.5-2m; H c. 2-c.5m). The main entrance, with indications of a gatehouse, is at the N end of the W wall. There is a second, probably relatively modern, entrance in the centre of the N wall. There are projecting D-shaped, single-storey towers at the E end of the N wall and in the centre of the S wall. There are a series of blocked-up gun loops in the bawn walls and in at least one of the towers. The enclosed area is densely overgrown with vegetation. However a number of low walls, probably of relatively recent origin, are visible. A short distance away is a house, probably of late 16th/early 17th century date (SL019-062001-). 

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

The remains comprise a rectangular, single-storey house (13.65m E-W; 6m N-S; Wall T 0.6m) with high gable ends and two large butresses on the S wall. There is a doorway (Wth 0.95m) E of the centre in the S wall. There are two large windows to the W of the doorway and one to the E. Located W of the centre in the N wall is a massive fireplace flanked by large windows. There are smaller fireplaces in each of the gables. There are two small rooms at the E end of the house and a single larger room at W. There is a bawn (SL019-062002-) associated with a levelled castle (SL019:062001-) c. 25m SE.

source_data.original_text:
Situated at the summit of Red Hill affording panoramic views in all directions. Circular platform (diam. 30m) enclosed by a substantial, although largely collapsed, wall of drystone masonry (Wth 5.5-6m; H 1m). An external facing of large blocks may still be traced at the S half of the cashel and at N and NE. Original entrance may have been at E. From NW-N-NE, 10-15m out from the external foot of the cashel wall, is a substantial bank of earth and stone (Wth 5m; H 1m) with an external fosse (Wth 4-5.7m) and outer bank (Wth 5m; H 1.25m). Both banks have evidence for internal and external stone revetment. From SE-S-SW only the largely levelled remains of the inner bank is still traceable. Both banks and fosse are absent at W where the site is defended by the naturally-occurring steep slope of the hill. They are also absent at E. A rectangular pit (7.5m NW-SE; 3.6m NE-SW) has been dug into the inner face of the first bank at N. The cashel is divided into unequal portions by a NE-SW field boundary. Built beneath or against the inner face of the cashel wall is a souterrain (SL019-064002-). There is a hut site (SL019-064003-) 100m E. Much of the upper reaches of Red Hill are occupied by an disused field system (SL019-064004-) of uncertain antiquity. 

Attached image: SL019-064001_01 Location of cashel viewed from N

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

In average pasture with some rock outcrop on the S-facing slope of Red Hill. This enclosure survives as a D-shaped terrace (41m N-S; 35-40m E-W) cut into the naturally-occurring S-facing slope. It is defined on on its straight W side by a field wall. From N-NNE-NE it is defined by the curving line of a S-facing scarp (H 0.9m) which peters out to the E. A far more substantial S-facing scarp (H 2m) defines the terrace from SSW-S-SE. There is no enclosing element at E. This feature is now largely occupied by a concrete-built barn with associated cattle enclosure. The smaller fields that comprised a field system (SL019-069003-) and the second enclosure (SL019-069002-) have been levelled.

The interior area is not noticeably raised above exterior ground level and is wet and boggy underfoot. Several metres to the SW and W of the monument is a possible field system (SL019-071001-).

The possibility that the building dates to pre-1700 AD cannot be ruled out
Listed in the SMR (1989) (1987) and RMP (1995) (1997)

source_data.original_text:
Situated on the N side of the road within the old demesne of Longford House. The building is depicted on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map but without the designation 'Old Chapel' which it has on the current edition (1913). The remains are those of a small gabled, single-storey, rectangular building, roofed with slate (4.60m x 1.60m internally; wall thickness 0.45-0.55m). The structure, built of mortared stone and aligned NNW-SSE, is entered by an arched doorway (1.62m H; 0.70m W) in the N gable wall. The upper portion of the building appears to have been rebuilt and the slated roof added, probably in the 20th cent. The E wall is pierced by an arched opening and there is a narrow ope (H 0.44m) in the upper portion of the S gable. It is not possible to accurately determine the function or date of the building but it would appear to be an ornamental feature typcial of 18th century demesnes and may well have been built to house some of the stone carvings set into its walls (SL019-093002-). It is most unlikely to have been used as a chapel - the space within can accommodate little more than two individuals. The possibility that the building dates to pre-1700 AD cannot be ruled out. Listed in the SMR (1989) (1987) and RMP (1995) (1997) as 'Chapel'. (Wood-Martin 1882, I, 116-8; Foras Forbartha report 1973 and 1979).

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Situated in 'Loughanacrannoge' a shallow basin of wet marshy ground which holds a pool of water in the winter months. The crannog comprises a small circular raised area (diam. 12m; H 1.2m) which is densely overgrown with long grass and scrub. Wood-Martin (1886, 246) recorded that 'a trench cut through the island showed that it was composed of clay mingled with some few stones, and these, around the exterior edge, were arranged in a systematic manner'. At the S of the crannog a depression (Wth. 0.8m), partially infilled with stones, is visible. This may be the remnants of the cutting referred to by Wood-Martin. (OS Letters 1836, 322 (135)).

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a rise, with a steep slope on its W side, in otherwise undulating pasture. Raised circular platform (diam. 34.3m) enclosed by a very substantial bank of earth and stone (Wth. 7.6m - 9.6m; int. H 0.9m - 1.6m) atop a mound of earth and stone (H 1.3m - 2.7m). A field boundary wall has been constructed on top of the bank from W-N-NE. At the foot of the mound is a fosse (Wth. 2m - 2.5m) with an outer bank (Wth. 6.2m; H 1.3m). Fosse and outer bank are well preserved from NW-N-E but elsewhere only faint remains are visible. From SW-W-WNW the outer bank has been incorporated into a N-S field boundary wall. Break in bank at E (Wth. 3m) probably represents original entrance. Outside is an area of disturbance, incorporating field clearance stones, which extends towards a corresponding break in the outer bank. Projecting out from the bank at N is a raised U-shaped area (dims. 34m N-S; 25.5m E-W) defined by a scarp (H 0.6m - 1.4m). Its E and W sides are relatively straight and its N side curved. At the E side the scarp is kerbed with stone. Within the E quadrant is a hollow (dims. 8m E-W; 10.2m N-S) which may be a quarry hole.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Shown as 'stone circle' on the OS 6 inch map (1913). Wood-Martin (1887-8, 256-7) describes the site as a slightly raised mound 'c. 57' N-S by 45' E-W '; 'formerly encircled with boulders'. He records that the site was traditionally called 'Coolcrave' and was said to be the burial place of those who died in a battle which took place nearby. The extant remains consist of a semi-circular level area, c. 18m N-S. defined on the NW-E-S by remnants of a ring of close-set boulders and incorporated into a curving field wall on the S-E and NE. The stones survive best in the NW-N where six to seven boulders occur in a curving line. In the S five close set boulders appear also to be in situ and a there are a few isolated stones protruding from the overgrowth on the E. The boulders have a maximum dimension of 0.50m-0.70m, and vary in height from 0.40m to 0.80m. The W half of the site has been obliterated and on this side the site is now bordered by a rough track immediately to the W from which the ground falls away sharply. (Bergh 1995, 219, 222)

Compiled by: Geraldine Stout

source_data.original_text:
Situated at the base of a slope at the source of an ENE-flowing stream within a heavily-wooded thicket. The well has dried up. Remains comprise a circular setting of stones (diam. 2m). The well is said to have been created by St. Feichin of Ballisodare, and to have been the place where he frequently met his brother St. Adamanan of Skreen (OS Letters 1836, 319 (132). Patterns here ceased in the 1860s. A stone (SL019-141003-) bearing the track of St. Feichin's knees is said to have been located within the well (ITA Survey 1942-4). There is a tradition of a cross or cross inscribed stone (SL019-141002-) at this site (Timoney M.A. pers. comm. 1989). Neither the stone bearing the track of St. Feichin's knees nor the cross were located.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on an E-W ridge with a pronounced N-facing slope, with excellent views of the surrounding hilly terrain. Large oval area (57.7m E-W; 51.2m N-S) defined by remnants of a substantial stony bank, enhanced on the N side by the steep ridge slope. The curving arc of the bank (Wth 4-5.9m; int. H 0.6-1.3m; ext. H 1.7-2m) at SW-NNW is well defined.  At NW it peters out where the defining element becomes a scarp merging at NNW–NNE with the steep natural ridge slope (H 5.6m). At NE–E remnants of a stony bank are evident, replaced at ESE-S-SSW by a later field wall (Wth 1.2; H 0.6 at S), now ruined and largely obscured by blackthorn and brambles. A gap (Wth 2m) at E may represent the original entrance. The interior incorporates a central E-W spine of raised level ground (Wth c. 15-20m N–S) from which interior ground level falls steeply towards the perimeter at N, and more gently at S. This level central spine appears to reflect the natural undulations of the ridge. It is broadest at the E end of the enclosure, and here there is a rectangular platform (12.5m E-W; 10.8m N-S), which appears to be the remains of a house (SL019-149002-). A ruined field wall (W 1-1.3m; H 0.7m), engulfed in brambles, extends on an ENE–WSW axis through the S third of the enclosure. The enclosure is boxed in on all sides by later field boundary walls. At W a field wall, which lies 3m outside the enclosure bank, respects the curve of the enclosure, possibly preserving the line of a fosse or outer bank. There is a church (SL019-150001-) and graveyard (SL019-150002-) c. 170m to SE

Attached image (SL019-149001-_01 shows enclosure viewed from N.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Situated within a hollow at the base of a steep N-facing ridge are two adjoining holy wells dedicated to St. Patrick and St. Brigid respectively, within a small, square walled enclosure (dim. 11m). Patterns are still held here annually on June 29th. This, the larger well is dedicated to St. Patrick and comprises a circular pool (diam. 2m) defined by a stone wall. Four stone steps lead down to the water level. Appended to its W side is 'St. Brigid's Well' (SL019-151002-) roofed by a massive slab which bears numerous crudely inscribed crosses (SL019-151003-). A series of stone steps leads down to the water level. Built into the enclosure wall, a short distance SW of the wells, is a stone crucifixion plaque (SL019-151004-). Also within the enclosure is a plain rectangular stone altar (SL019-151005-). A third well, which was used by penitents for washing their feet before and after undertaking the patterns, is located 1.7m N of the enclosure.

source_data.original_text:
In forestry on the N slopes of the Ox Mountains, located on a natural knoll, on a shelf of rough, upland terrain, overlooked to S by cliffs. This record was listed in the RMP (1995) as ‘Miscellaneous’. It refers to a setting of stones inspected in 1967 in advance of forestry development (SMR Files), and recorded as follows: ‘Rough heathery ground full of boulders. About 10 small boulders in a row (N–S) with 4 or 5 at right angles at N end. Like footing of wall of shelter...Not a megalith. Not ancient looking.’ An inspection was carried out in 1994 but the feature was not located due to forestry cover. The area was inspected again in 2014. The knoll is thickly covered in heather and rough scrub. The top and parts of the slopes are strewn with a dense jumble of felled timber. Young trees grow on the slopes and around the perimeter. Occasional boulders and stones protrude randomly from the heather and forestry debris. On the gentle N-facing slope, just below the top of the knoll, four stones (max. dims. c. 0.5m; H 0.3m) in a close-set N-S row (L c. 2m) can be glimpsed/felt beneath thick heather. It is not possible to determine if these stones are a remnant of the structure, which may have been partly or entirely destroyed during forestry works.

source_data.original_text:
The building is indicated though not named on both the 1837 and 1910 editions of the OS 6-inch maps. The remains comprise a single-storey, vaulted structure (6.25m L x 3.50m W internally) with walls 1.25m T. The walls stand to c. 2m high and the building is c. 4m high to the apex of the gable. The W wall contains three openings, 2 splayed loops flanking a wider central one - possibly a window - the outer stonework is missing so it is impossible to know the external width of the opening: the S of these three opes is blocked up. There are three comparable openings in the E wall. The N and middle one are splayed and the S one appears to be the remains of a wall-press; its sides do not appear to be splayed. The outer ends of these opes are damaged and blocked up.
There is no evidence for a window/opening in the S gable. Set about mid-way in the exterior face is a stone with a hole. Although it superficially looks like a gun-loop it is not splayed or regularly dressed. In addition, there is no evidence of an opening at this point on the interior of the wall and it would appear that this stone was inserted here. More than likely it originally served as the footing stone for the pintle of a door. 
The entrance to the building is via a pointed doorway (W 1.05m, H 1.60m) in the centre of the N wall. Only the upper part of the doorway is visible on the exterior, the lower being obscured by a mound of stone and gravel placed there to hinder access to the building (pers comm. landowner). The stones forming the doorway are all dressed with large punch marks typical of 16th/17th century work. The doorway is slightly battered and this is retained in the stonework for c. 0.50m on either side where it is then set back to the vertical. There is a local tradition that both the doorway and armorial stone set in the wall above it (SL019-200003-) were brought here from the old 'castle' to the W. However, while it seems likely that the armorial stone is certainly an insertion, the doorway, more than likely, is in situ and formed part of the original building.
This building is described in the Buildings of architectural interest in Co. Sligo (An Foras Forbartha, 1973, p. 22) as a '17th century chapel' and in the subsequent edition of same (1979, p. 56) as 'apparently an early-17th century chapel, but so rustic as to give little indication as to its function, perhaps more likely a gate-lodge.' It is most unlikely that this building ever functioned as a gate-lodge and its identification as a 'chapel' would appear to be based on a miss-reading by the compiler of the report of the OS 6-inch map. The compiler appears to have linked the name 'Old Chapel' with this building rather than with that to the east in the grounds of Longford House. This interpretation of events is reinforced by the fact that the reference in the report to the latter building makes no mention of it as being a chapel. The vaulted building has clear affinities with tower-house rather than church architecture and, in addition, it is aligned N-S, an atypical orientation for a church. Wood-Martin recorded the tradition that it once served as a forge (1882, I, 118) and this would explain the flue-hole broken through the apex of the vault about two-thirds of the way S of the entrance: above this sits the chimney. It is difficult to assign a date to the building with any accuracy though the use of the punch dressing on the doorway would indicate a date in the later 16th/early 17th century.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

Set in the N wall above the doorway of a late-medieval building (SL019-200001-) is an armorial stone (0.74m H x 0.65m W) bearing the much-weathered arms, crest and motto of the Crofton family, all represented within a roundel delineated by a raised band; the carving is in shallow false relief. At the lower end of the roundel may be discerned the faint traces of a crudely-carved lion, passant, guardant (the Crofton arms) and directly above is a seven-branched stalk of wheat (the crest). Traces of the family motto 'Dat Deus Incrementum' can be read, especially within the band at the top where the letters DEUS and INCRE are clearly discernible. In the top right-hand corner are remnants of an ornamental design comprising two curving terminals with a leaf-shaped motif, almost like a crude fleur-de-lis; the corresponding ornament in the left-hand corner is completely worn away. The date of this piece is uncertain. The style of lettering is typical of that found in 17th cent. contexts but would not be out of character in the early 18th century.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a broad terrace, broken by limestone pavement, on the E side of Red or Skreen Hill. There is a rath (SL019-013----) 25m to NW and a cashel (SL019-260----) 25m to W. 
This souterrain consists of three well-built, interconnected chambers, in a roughly N−S line, constructed using both drystone and rock-cut techniques.
At surface level a low, grass-covered linear rise (L 7-8m; Wth c. 1.5-2m; H 0.5) is visible. At the N end of the linear rise, there is a shallow, grassed-over sunken feature (1m N–S; 0.7m E-W; D 0.5m), faced on the W and N by drystone walling (H 0.4-0.5m). This may to be the remnants of an original entrance to the souterrain. At the S end of this sunken feature, there is an opening (Wth 0.7m; H 0.4m) into a short constriction or creep (L 0.6m N–S), roofed by a single lintel. It opens into the N end of a subrectangular chamber (Chamber 1) (L 1.25m; W 1.1m; H 1.33m at S end), with walls of drystone construction, roofed by a N-S row of three lintels. The E wall is straight, but the W wall curves inwards gently, so that the N end of the chamber narrows to the width of the entrance creep. The entrance creep, which is just below exterior ground level, opens into the chamber at the level of the lintelled roof. Soil and loose rubble of medium and large-sized stones infill the chamber, sloping down from the entrance creep to the base of the S wall of the chamber. This sloping infill conceals the original floor surface and part of the chamber walls. The slope highlights the discrepancy in height of c. 0.9-1m between the entrance creep, and floor level at the S end of the chamber, and it seems likely that it mirrors the original floor, which must slope down or be stepped in some way from N to S.
At the W end of the S wall of Chamber 1, at floor level, there is another creep (L 0.6m; Wth 0.56m at base, 0.45m at top; H 0.53m at N end, 0.66m at S end). It is roofed with two lintels, resting on side walls which differ in construction: the E wall is formed of a single upright slab; the W wall is rock-cut at its base, above which there is drystone masonry, which inclines inwards gently towards the top.
The creep opens into the middle of the N wall of Chamber 2 (L 1.97 NNE−SSW; Wth 1.58m; H 1.57m), which is subrectangular in plan. The lower portion (H 0.45-0.6m) of the walls are rock-cut, above which there is drystone walling. The walls incline inwards gently towards the top, and the upper course incorporates large limestone blocks, serving as corbels to support a row of three roof lintels. Towards the S end of the W wall, at a height of c. 0.7m above floor level, there is a rectangular recess or wall cupboard (Wth 0.3m; H 0.3m; D 0.4m) roofed with a single large stone block. The floor of Chamber 2 is covered with a mix of earth and loose stone rubble, which appears to be intrusive to a depth of at least 0.2m.
In the centre of the S wall of Chamber 2, there is a creep (L 0.5m N−S; Wth 0.48m; H 0.54m) roofed by a single lintel. The W wall is formed by a single upright slab, and the E wall is drystone walling.
The creep opens into the W end of the N wall of Chamber 3 (L 1.72m N−S; Wth 1.58m; H at least 1.5m), which is subrectangular in plan. The construction of the walls is similar to that of Chamber 2, with the lower levels (H 0.3-0.55m) cut from bedrock, above which there is drystone walling; in the S or back wall the bedrock rises to a height of c. 1.15m, reaching to just below roof level. Chamber 3 is roofed by three lintels of unequal size, the largest two covering the bulk of the roof space, with a third, narrow lintel at the N end. There is a well-built rectangular recess (H 0.23m; Wth 0.28m; D 0.44m) in the W wall, close to the NW corner, at a height of 0.85m above current floor level. In the SE corner of the chamber, just above floor level, there is a small natural opening (Wth 0.3m; H 0.2m) into an inaccessible fissure in the bedrock. The floor of the Chamber 3 is covered with earth and loose medium to large-sized stones.

In pasture, situated within a naturally-occurring depression of wet ground, bordered at S by a N-facing escarpment, and 15m to N by a low knoll upon which a rath (SL019-055----) is sited. The S shoreline of Ballisadare Bay is c.100m to N. A field drain (Wth 1.4m) curves in a shallow arc SE-N through the wet hollow. Along the S arc of the drain, a layer (L 14m; T 0.4-0.6m) of shattered stones within a charcoal-rich matrix is exposed in section at a depth of 0.4m-0.5m beneath present ground level. The layer is clearly visible in the N section face of the drain but only intermittently in the S section face. It overlies orange and pale grey subsoil layers. An animal bone was visible in dark-brown sandy soil at a level 0.15m above the burnt layer in the N section. There is a short interruption to the layer at its W end, at the point where the drain begins to curve to the N, but burnt material (L 8m) is again visible in both section faces where the drain extends to N. In the W section face a shallow dip in the surface of the burnt stone layer is filled with a grey, slightly greasy deposit (L 1m; T 0.15m) which is partly overlain by a lens of oyster shell (L 1m; T 0.15m). No trace of a mound is evident at surface level in the field but upcast from the drain, incorporating burnt mound material, has been spread on either side of the drain and heaped on top of the field fence that borders the W side of the drain.

source_data.original_text:
Incorporated into the garden of a house, with rising ground immediately to W and a road immediately to S. A T-plan church, annotated ‘R. C. Chapel (in Ruins’), is shown on the 1837 and the 1913 OS 6-inch maps. The transepts, which make up the bar of the 'T', are aligned E–W and the nave or shaft of the 'T' extends to the S. The church is constructed of mortared random rubble. The total N–S length appears to have been c. 17m, and total E–W length c. 16-17m. The roofless ruins comprise the W transept and the nave. The gable (L 6.2m N–S) of the W transept is intact and has a central pointed-arch window. The side walls (Wth 0.6m) of this transept survive to a height of 1.4m and a length of 5-6m E–W. A shed overlies, and possibly incorporates, the N wall of the E transept. There is no trace of the remainder of the E transept. The end or S wall (Wth 7m E–W) of the nave has a central blocked up doorway. The W side wall (L 10.5m N–S) of the nave is intact. The E side wall extends N from the end wall for 4m, decreasing in height towards its N end which has a cut-stone stoup (bowl diam. 0.3m) cemented onto it. The church probably dates to late 18th- or early 19th-century.

source_data.original_text:
Human remains were discovered during excavation for a slurry pit on a farm at Skreen More in November 1989. The skeletons had been exposed in the side of the cutting at a depth of 0.5m below the original ground level. All had been extensively damaged by the digger. The burials appear to have been orientated E-W and lay at intervals of 0.10m - 1.50m apart. There were no traces of burial structures or grave goods and the trench was backfilled. A ruined medieval parish church (SL019-007001-) is located just c. 110m to W of where the burials were found and a holy well, dedicated to St.Adamnáin, c. 65m to N. (Cahill and Sikora 2011, Vol. 2, 514)

source_data.original_text:
Situated on the E side of a peat-covered plateau on Knockachree Mountain in the Ox Mountains at an altitude of c. 538m OD. The ground falls away sharply c. 20m to the E of the monument. The views to the N to SSW are restricted due to peat banks along horizon, but there are excellent views in all other directions with the Bricklieves, Knocknashee, Knocknarea, Croagh Patrick and the E Ox Mountain range clearly visible.
The remains consist of a roughly circular cairn (c. 16.8m E-W; 17.2m N-S) that is partially buried in peat, especially along the E and SE sectors. Its highest point is c. 2.6m from SE edge. The cairn is best preserved in the SW quadrant and there is a considerable amount of cairn slippage along the E side: two OS trigonometrical stations, consisting of small circular heaps of stones (diam. 1.5-2m; H 0.7-1m), were built on its highest points. The N sector of the cairn has been quarried out exposing an area c. 8m (N-W) by 5m (E-W). Four possible kerbstones are visible along this N edge and three possible orthostats are exposed near the centre of this area.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in terrain broken by limestone pavement on a SE-facing slope on the E side of Red Hill. There are extensive views NE–S over a broad sweep of lowlying grassland, with the Ox Mountains defining the horizon SE–S. There is a rath (SL019-013----) immediately to N, and a souterrain (SL019-203----) c. 20m to ENE. Roughly circular area (22m E-W; c. 20-21m N–S) defined by a low, ruined and largely sod-covered stone bank/wall (Wth c. 4m; H c. 0.4m, at W) which is barely discernible in parts. At S–SW an arc of stones is visible which represents the in situ basal course of the external wall face. At SW–NW the stone bank is bordered externally by a shallow depression (Wth 2-2.5m; D 0.3m). This depression is not evident elsewhere around the circuit and it is not clear if it represents a fosse, or perhaps a remnant of an old trackway that skirted the cashel. At NNW–NNE the stone bank is truncated or overlain by an E–W field wall, immediately to N of which is a rath (SL019-013---). The field wall obscures the relationship between the two enclosures. The interior of the cashel has an uneven surface with much stone/bedrock protruding. A drystone field wall, on a NNW–SSE axis, cuts across the W edge of the interior. Abutting the E face of this wall, in the SE quadrant of the cashel, there is a stony depression (4m N–S; 0.6-1m E–W; D 0.5m).

This levelled burnt mound is evident as a concentration of small, angular stone fragments in a matrix of black, charcoal-rich soil, exposed for a length of 2.8m NW–SE on the low, eroded N bank of the stream/drain. It is located at a point where the flow of the stream changes direction from NW to NNW. At this point, a small causeway has been created by channelling the stream through a short length of concrete pipe, and infilling the stream gully/drain (Wth 1.4; D 0.4-0.5) with stones. The use of this crossing point by farm stock and farm machinery has eroded the grass cover on the stream bank and exposed a portion of the burnt mound. The full extent of the burnt mound cannot be traced on the flat, grass-covered ground to N of the steam.

source_data.original_text:
In blanket bog, located on the N edge of Knockachree Mountain, in the Ox Mountain Range. To N of the cairn the ground shelves away, dropping in steep terraces to the rocky cliffs that define the N edge of the mountain. The location provides panoramic views, encompassing the entire lowlying coastal strip from Killala Bay, Co. Mayo at NW to Sligo Bay at NE, and stretching N to Slieve League in Donegal. Benbulben and Knocknarae mountains are prominent to NE. To SE−SW the views are of the blanket bog-covered plateau of the mountain.
Subcircular cairn (18.6m N−S; 16m E−W) constructed of medium and large angular slabs of locally-occurring quartz-bearing gneiss/schist. The centre of the cairn appears to have been dug into/disturbed in the past, leaving a moss-covered stony hollow interior (5m N−S; 4.5m E−W) surrounded by an outer ring of cairn material. The outer ring consists of a stone bank (Wth c. 6m; H 1-1.4m) of irregular height, partly moss-covered. A small, roughly conical heap (diam.  3-3.5m; H 0.9m) of stones, has been built on top of the S edge of the cairn; it is of relatively recently construction, probably for use as a trigonometrical station. There is another cairn (SL019-258----) c. 600m to S, not visible from this cairn.
