source_data.original_text:
In good coastal grassland, 1km S of Ballysadare Bay; on elevated ground with a slope down to E.
This rath is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. A modern stone wall on a NNE−SSW axis crosses the rath to W of centre, coinciding with the boundary between the townlands of Carrownacreey at W and Tanrego West at E. The portion of the rath to W of the wall is in a pasture field; it survives as a barely discernible D-shaped platform. The larger portion lying to E of the wall is in deciduous woodland, its outline largely obscured by widely spaced mature beech trees and a close-set planting of young oaks.
Circular area (diam. c. 45m) defined by a levelled bank/scarp. The levelled bank can be traced as a low rise (Wth c. 3m; int. H 0.1m; ext. H 0.3-0.4m) on the NE arc. It is reduced to a low, uneven scarp (H 0.5m) on the SE−SW arc, becoming increasingly indistinct at W−NW, petering out at NNW−N (on the W side of the transecting wall), where it fades into a small area of wettish ground. There is an uneven sunken break (Wth c. 6m) in the scarp at E, which appears to have been partly dug out/disturbed in the modern era, and another break (Wth c. 2.4m) in the scarp at S.
A shallow depression (Wth 2-2.5m) immediately outside the scarp at S may indicate a fosse but cannot be traced elsewhere. 
To W of the transecting wall, the interior is level; it is grass-covered with ephemeral E-W linear features, possibly relict cultivation ridges. To E of the wall, the interior slopes gradually down to E and has an uneven surface, broken by a few large boulders; a post and wire fence extends to E from the N-S wall across the S half. An area of disturbance is evident in the N half, a mature tree stands adjacent to this, at the base of which is a concentration of moss-covered stones.
There is a souterrain (SL019-264002-) in the N half of the interior, close to the enclosing bank in the NE quadrant.
Relict field boundaries intersect with the rath at SW and E, and appear to post-date it.

source_data.original_text:
In a rath (SL019-264001-), close to the NE arc of the enclosing bank. 
A vertical lintelled opening (Wth c. 0.58m; H 0.46m) reveals a small subterranean cavity or chamber (c. 0.8m NW-SE; c. 1.2m NE-SW) with drystone sidewalls and a linteled roof. The chamber appears to be roughly D-shaped in plan, with the opening on the straight SE-facing side.
The drystone sidewalls at N and S incline inwards to support two roof lintels (in E-W row); the base of these walls is not visible due to an infill of soil. The back (NW) wall does not have stone facing, exposing an earthen ‘wall’; it seems likely that the originally stone-faced has collapsed here –much of now forming the earth and stone infill in the base of the chamber.
A small square recess (Wth 0.3m; D c. 0.45m; H 0.3m) is built into the N wall. The E and W sidewalls of the recess are each formed by a large blocky stone, the back wall is of drystone masonry using smaller stones; it is roofed with a slab. The floor is a thin slab, keyed into the E wall but barely reaching the W sidewall. Beneath this slab is another shallower cavity (H 0.15m), giving the impression that the recess is split-level. 
A domed heap of earth and stones fills the base of the chamber, concealing the original floor and the base of the sidewalls. It is impossible, therefore, to determine the original height of the chamber, but it was at least 0.75m. This loose infill is highest in a central E−W spine, rising to within 0.5m of the roof lintels. 
The S sidewall continues as a very low, sod-concealed wall beyond the chamber opening for 0.55m to SE, ending at a short turn to S. It partly defines the S side of a shallow surface depression (Wth c. 0.95m N−S) that extends to SE of the chamber for c. 2m before petering out. Apart from the short length of walling on the S side, mentioned above, this depression is defined at N and S by a low earthen scarp with no trace of stone facing.
The remains appear to be a souterrain. The visible ‘chamber’ is small and difficult to interpret. What we see is most likely only a portion of a larger structure and it is not possible to be certain now of its original form and extent. The infilling soil may conceal an opening to a continuation of the souterrrain NW into the rising slope, and the shallow surface depression in front chamber suggests a possible continuation to SE.

Centrally located within the internal area of a rath (SL022-004001-) is a circular raised area (diam. 10m; H 0.7-1m), corresponing with the location marked 'Funnel' on the 1837 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps. Beneath this, and extending from it in a SW direction, is a collpased and partially infilled, drystone-built passage (L 9m; Wth 3m; H 1.2m). At its SW end is a D-shaped drystone-built chamber (4.85m NNE-SSW; 2.85m WNW-ESE; H 2.2m) whose lintel roof has partially collapsed. At floor level at the N end of the E (straight) wall of the chamber is a small lintelled opening (Wth 0.95m; H 0.45m) which gives access to a largely collapsed passage. At the SSW corner of the chamber is a second low, lintelled opening (Wth 0.75m; H 0.4m) at floor level giving access to a second passage which appears to extends to S. The line of this passage appears to be indicated at surface level by a shallow, depression located 5m S of the collapsed D-shaped chamber. A sketch plan of the souterrain in the OS Name Books (vol. 1, p. 215) shows this passage extending to the rath bank at S to the point marked 'Mouth of Cave on the 1837 OS 6-inch map and 'Cave' on the 1913 edition.

source_data.original_text:
Situated in level pasture. Rectangular, three storey with attic, gable-ended, limestone built structure (19.8m ENE-WSW; 9m NNW-SSW ; Wall T 1.5m) with base batter. At ground floor level there are three slit opes in the SSE wall, two in the WSW wall and two in the NNW wall. All, with the exception of one round-headed example in the NNW wall, are square headed and chamfered. All have had their embrasures filled in. The original entrance is in the centre of the SSE wall. A large, broken-out opening in the NNW wall may mark a secondary entrance. The modern entrance is in the centre of the ENE wall. At first floor level there are two slit opes with hood-moulding in the ENE wall. There is one square-headed and chamfered window in the SSE wall and two in the WSW wall. In the NNW and SSE walls are four and three large rectangular windows respectively. These are later insertions. At second floor level there are single slit opes in the ENE, SSE, and WSW walls. In the NNW and SSE walls there are four and 3 large rectangular windows respectively. These are later insertions. Access to the battlements is via a round-headed, two-centred doorway at the SSE end of the ENE wall. There are large chimney stacks at each gable and a walk-way between the chimney stacks and the battlements. There are bartizans at the WNW and ESE angles. There are large blocked-up fireplaces in both gables at 1st and 2nd floor levels. The floors were supported by corbels. Draughting on the corbels and on other stonework suggests that the structure dates to around the middle of the 17th century.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
In a modern Catholic church at Corbally. Cross constructed from a single block of stone (H 0.76m; max. Wth. at arms. 0.42m; T 0.14-0.16m) with carvings in relief on both faces, and a short tang (D 0.05m) at the base of the cross. On one side is a depiction of the crucifixion. The carving of the figure of Christ shows simplified facial features and a loin cloth. Nails are shown piercing each hand and a single nail pierces the overlapping feet. Beneath the feet is a skull. On the other side of the cross is a depiction of a ladder, which extends the full length of the cross, and hammer and tongs, which are carved on one arm of the cross. The original location (SL0016-071----) of the cross is said to be in Carrowcardin townland where a church, marked 'R. C. Chapel' is shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map (Mary Timoney 1989, pers. comm.).

source_data.original_text:
Depicted as a cluster of three dwellings on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map where they are named 'Bellanaboy (ruins)': the name is not in antiquarian typeface. Wood-Martin in his 'History of Sligo, county and town (1882, vol. 1, pp. 115-6) refers to 'a map of the barony, circum. 1609,' where 'twenty-three castes were marked. Most of these have totally disappeared … there are slight remains of buildings at ….. Bellanaboy…' The compilers of the SMR (1989) identified the 'buildings' marked on the OS 6-inch map (1837) as the site of this castle. On inspection in 1993 no visible remains of any structure resembling a 'castle' were found at this location. It is impossible to know if Wood-Martin ever visited this site; it is possible that he inferred a connection between the location of the 'castle' on the 1609 map with the name recorded on the OS 6-inch map. It is evident that the buildings represented on the OS 6-inch map were in ruins at the time of the survey (1837) though it is impossible to determine their age. The possibility that they could be of pre-1700 AD date cannot be ruled out.

Revised by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 25 August 2011

The body of a middle-aged man was found at a depth of 0.8m below the surface in a bog in Tawnamore townland. The body, which was extended on its back, with the head to the SSE, lay on on birch twigs. A full set of well preserved woollen clothing was recovered, including a hat, overcoat, jacket, breeches, pair of knitted woollen socks, pair of garters and a pair of shoes: these are on display in the National Museum of Ireland. The style of the clothing suggested a date of the mid-17th-century. The location of the site of the discovery was verified in 2013 (pers. comm. M.A. Timoney). (Lucas 1972, 181-223; 215-222; Timoney and Heraughty 2002, 290-1)

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a low rise on top of a NW–SE ridge, giving good views across falling ground to W, and of the Ox Mountains which define the horizon to S. An oblong or sub-rectangular mound (7.7m N–S; 5.9m E–W; H 0.8m at N, 1.2m at E) with a flat top (Wth 3m E–W). The sides slope in two tiers, giving the effect of a low narrow step or terrace encircling the base of the mound. On the E side several close-set stones form a facing around the upper tier. There are two stones set against the base of the mound on the E side. A number of large stones lying on top of the mound are recent additions. According to local tradition, the mound is known as the ‘Cotteen’ and is said to be a burial site associated with the chiefs of the O’Callaghan clan.

source_data.original_text:
Locating in a field of rough pasture, bordered by bog to W, SW and NW. The field slopes gradually to E and S towards the valley of the Gowlan River. This record was not listed in the SMR (1989). It was listed in the RMP (1995) as ‘field wall –pre-bog’ but no source of information or field description was added to the file at that time. The area was inspected in 2014. The field,  appears to have been reclaimed from bog. The ground surface, covered in rough grass, rushes, and tufts of heather, is very uneven, with frequent heather-covered, peaty hummocks and much stone breaking the surface. The stones are low and largely obscured by moss, sod or heather, and in general appear to be randomly scattered. It is unclear whether the heather-covered hummocks conceal more stones. One possible linear feature was noted. It consists of a gapped line of stones and heathery hummocks covering a distance of c. 6m on a WNW–ESE axis. It is not possible to be certain that this represents the remains of a pre-bog field wall.

Skeleton Two comprised only some of the lower limb bones, which partly overlay those of Skeleton One. No features or textural difference in the surrounding peat suggested a grave structure or pit. raw_items.raw_text: used as a Protestant place of worship until 1812

source_data.original_text:
Located within a graveyard (SL012-036002-). Late medieval church, which gave its name to the parish of Kilmacshalgan, associated with a 13th century friary which continued in use until the friars were expelled by Cromwell (OS Name Books, 120). It was 'repaired' in 1615 and used as a Protestant place of worship until 1812 (O'Rorke 1890, 411; Kilgannon 1926, 297). Situated in level, lowlying pasture at the base of a NE-facing slope. Oriented WNW-ESE, the church is described here according to the E-W convention. It is rectangular in plan (ext. dims. c. 18m WNW-ESE; 7.53m NNE-SSW; Wall T 0.65-1m), with walls constructed of mortared limestone. In the E wall is a tall, rounded-headed window (H c. 3m). In the W wall is a blocked-up rectangular window above a recently renovated arched doorway. On the S side of the doorway is a drawbar socket. In the N wall are three, now blocked-up, large rectangular windows, each topped with a low arches of voussoirs. In the S wall are three featureless rectangular windows. The church is densely overgrown with ivy and brambles.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of revised upload: 12 November 2019

Not marked as an antiquity on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. Small, roughly trapezoidal promontory (18m NW-SE; c. 5m NE-SW) jutting into the S side of Sligo Bay. source_data.original_text:
This barrow, known locally as ‘The Moat’, was fully excavated in 1963 in advance of road-widening works on the N 59 Sligo-Ballina road (Danaher 1964). Prior to excavation the barrow appeared as a roughly circular mound (diam. 13.5m; H 2.3m), gently domed in profile, with a somewhat steeper slope near the summit on the W and N side. Excavation determined that the barrow was composed of a roughly circular cairn (diam. 11.85m; H 1.5m) of stones and gravel, with a kerb-like setting of stones at SW and NE, overlain by a mound of stony soil. There was no evidence of an enclosing fosse. The primary burial in the barrow was of an ox. It was unburnt and unprotected, lying slightly NW of centre, 0.25cm above the old ground level. Associated with the ox burial were twelve poorly-preserved sherds of pottery and a waste fragment of chert. A few other unburnt animal bones of calf, pig and ox were found within the lower layers of the cairn material. In a secondary phase of activity at the barrow, a cist (SL012-053002-) was inserted into the summit of the barrow on its W side, and a pit-burial (SL012-053003-) was inserted into the E side. Both contained cremated remains.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 7 May 2013

source_data.original_text: In an unclassified barrow (SL012-053001-). This cist was discovered when the barrow was fully excavated in 1963 in advance of road-widening works on the N 59 Sligo-Ballina road (Danaher 1964). The cist represented a secondary phase of activity at the barrow. A hole was dug into the summit of the barrow on its W side and the cist was constructed in the hole. The cist (L 0.45m; W 0.3m) was subrectangular in plan, with each of the four sides built of a double wall of small slabs set on edge. It was roofed by a single capstone (L 1m; Wth 0.85m; T 0.12m). The floor was paved with three slabs. The cist contained the cremated bones of an adult human of unknown gender. A waste flake of chert was found with the bones. A pit-burial (SL012-053003-), also containing cremated remains, was inserted into the E side of the barrow.

In an unclassified barrow (SL012-053001-). This pit-burial was discovered when the barrow was excavated in 1963 in advance of road-widening works on the N 59 Sligo-Ballina road (Danaher 1964, 145). The pit-burial, which represented a secondary phase of activity at the barrow, was inserted into the E side of the barrow. It consisted of a pit in which the cremated remains of an adult human of unknown gender were placed. Ccremated animal bones were also recovered and five decorated pottery sherds of Food Vessel type Food Vessel-like. Twelve fragments of chert were found in the vicinity of the pit-burial. (Danaher 1964, 145-158)

In pasture, located in wet ground at the base of a N-facing slope. This holy well is named Tobercahillboght on the 1837 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of a circular, steep sided hole (diam. 0.55m, D 0.8m) whose sides and floor are lined with stones. It is now dry. It is located 12m to SE of a natural spring, which emerges from the base of the slope and flows N into a small pool. There is a crucifix plaque (SL012-067002-), located within a small circle of stones, 2m E of the stone-lined well. 

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Located 2m to E of a holy well (SL012-067001-). A small stone crucifix (H 0.53m; Wth of arms 0.44m; Wth shaft 0.17m, T 0.007m) lies on the ground in the centre of a circle (diam. 2m) of loosely piled small stones. Carved in relief on one face of the cross is a depiction of Christ with simplified facial features and crossed feet. Diagaonal lines represent a loin cloth. The right arm of the cross bears the date 1749. The left arm, which has been broken off but lies adjacent to the cross, bears indecipherable symbols.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on an E-W rise or low ridge in pasture. The ground level falls away to the N. Large raised circular area (68.8m E-W; 66m N-S) defined by a scarp (ext. H 1.5m at E, 0.8m at W), with slight traces of the original bank (Wth c. 3.5m) at NW. The entrance is not clearly defined but may have been at SW where the internal ground level is lowest relative to the exterior. Within the SE quadrant is a possible house (SL012-068002-). The NW quadrant is separated from the remainder by a curving bank (Wth 3-3.5m; H 0.7-0.9m). Large stones set in the bank may be remnants of stone facing. Constructed against the inner face of this bank, within the SE portion of the area it encloses, are the remains of a possible house (SL012-068003-). The NW quadrant is further sub-divided by low bank which extends from the NW corner of the house site to the perimeter at NNW. There is a holy well (SL012-067001-) at the base of the slope c. 90m to N.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a naturally-occurring rise in pasture. Raised oval area (29.6m E-W; 26.8m N-S) enclosed by a substantial earthen bank (Wth 6m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 3.1m, at N) with a wide, deep external fosse (Wth 3.5m). At the outer lip of the fosse is a second bank (Wth 5.3m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 2m). At the outer foot of the second bank is a wide space (Wth 5m), probably an infilled fosse. At its outer edge at N and E is a modern field boundary, possibly an adaptation of a third bank. This has been levelled at S and W. A break (Wth 3m) in the inner bank at E, with a corresponding break (Wth 2m) in outer bank, represents the original entrance. Stones protruding from the inner face of the inner bank may be remnants of a facing or kerb. There is a local tradition of a souterrain (SL012-071002-) in the interior of the rath. There is a mound (SL012-071003-) c. 30m SSE of the rath.


Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 19 January 2011

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a gentle ESE-facing slope, c. 60m W of a small stream, in reclamed pasture. Raised circular area (diam. 20.1m) enclosed by two low banks of earth and stone with shallow intermediate fosse. The inner bank (Wth 0.2-0.8m) and the fosse (Wth. 3.1m) are present for the complete circuit. The outer bank (Wth c.3m; H 0.5m) has been levelled from N-WNW but its outline can still be traced from N-E. Large quantities of stone were used in the construction of both banks. Large facing stones have been applied to both the inner and outer faces of both banks. There is a blocked-up, stone-lined break (Wth. 1.8m) in the inner bank at SSW, probably marking the original entrance. The interior is quite waterlogged and is populated by reeds and other scrub.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, straddling the level top and gentle SE-facing slope of a broad low hill. Ground falls away gently towards the Ballybeg River c. 100m to E. The hill and the surrounding field are dotted with boulders/erratics. Subcircular area (53m N–S; 53m E–W) enclosed by an earth and stone bank (Wth 1.8-2m; int. H 0.65-1.1m; ext. H 0.75-0.8m). The bank is composed of a core of earth and stone with a rough facing of large rounded or irregular-shaped boulders. The degree of preservation of the bank is variable and there are several breaks, or severely eroded sections, including breaks at NE (Wth 4m), E (3m), S (3m) and SW (c. 10m), NW (Wth 3m). In the N half of the interior there is a slight slope down from NW to SE but ground levels out in the S half. A subrectangular area (19m N-S; 22.5m E-W) in the SE quadrant of the interior is partitioned off by a bank of earth and stone, now very degraded. A large prostrate stone (min. L 2.7m; min. Wth 1m), possibly bedrock, protrudes from the sod in the W half of the partitioned area. A break (Wth 3m), in the enclosure bank at S, allow access into the partitioned off area. A field wall of boulders extends for 18m to S from the SW edge of the enclosure, and remnants of another possible field boundary (L 7m N-S; Wth 1.2-2m; H 0.4m) abuts the enclosure at S. These field boundaries are part of a field system (SL011-032002-), fragmentary remains of which traverse the hill. There is a mound (SL011-032001-) immediately to NW of the enclosure.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 13 November 2013

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the top of a broad low hill. Ground falls away gently towards the Ballybeg River c. 100m to E. The location provides extensive views of the surrounding gently undulating coastal pastureland, with the sea visible in the distance to N, the Ox Mountains on the skyline to SE, and Nephin Mountain and the Nephin Beg range visible on the far horizon to SW. A low, roughly D-shaped earthen mound (14m N–S; 10m E–W) which may originally have been circular. It has a gently domed profile, with a slightly flattened top which grades gently into broadly sloping sides (H 0.6m at S, 1.3m at W and N) at SE–N. The straight side is at E. Here the slope is very shallow and grades seamlessly into the surrounding ground level so that the limits of the mound on this side are difficult to define. It is not shown on OS 6-inch maps but the location is marked as a trigonometrical station (145 feet OD) on 1913 edition. Immediately to SSW of the mound there is a large enclosure (SL011-032----). Fragmentary remains of a field system (SL011-032002-) can be traced across the hill. 

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 31 December 2013

source_data.original_text:
In pasture/grazing, on the level top and the gentle slopes of a broad low hill. Ground falls away gently towards the Ballybeg River c. 100m to E. The hill and the surrounding area are dotted with boulders/erratics. Fragmentary remains of a field system are visible in the vicinity of an enclosure (SL011-032----) and a mound (SL011-032001-). One field boundary intersects with the enclosing stone-faced bank of the enclosure at SW. This field boundary (Wth 1.5-2m; H 0.6-0.8), which appear as a linear sod-covered rise incorporating large boulders, extends for 18m to S of the enclosure. Intersecting with it is a short length (c. 3m E–W) of a perpendicular field boundary which extends to E. Fragments of other field walls on an E-W axis can be discerned c. 30m to E and SE. Linear concentarions of boulders, which may be remnants of field boundaries also occur to NW of the enclosure, located immediately to W of the mound (SL011-032001-), and c. 90m to SW of the enclosure. The field boundary which intersects with the SW of the enclosure is shown on the 1913 OS 6-inch map but the field system as a whole is not shown on that edition or on the earlier 1837 edition. The extant remains are too scattered and fragmentary to allow reconstruction of the original pattern and size of the fields.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 21 January 2014
